## DAILY SECURITY BRIEFING

### 1. Europe expands military support as Ukraine’s air defenses run low
The European Commission approved €6.1 billion for Ukrainian air and missile defenses, ammunition and radars. Britain will permit the release of classified information on components of the SCALP/Storm Shadow missile to support production in Ukraine, while France pledged additional interceptor missiles.  
**Why it matters:** Ukraine reports a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors as Russian ballistic-missile attacks intensify. European measures could strengthen both immediate defenses and Ukraine’s longer-term domestic weapons production.

### 2. Ukraine broadens deep-strike operations inside Russia
Ukraine said it struck an Iskander ballistic-missile launcher near its border, part of a new effort to destroy launch systems because interceptor stocks are limited. Ukrainian drones also reportedly hit Russian fighter aircraft, air-defense systems and radars, while attacks continued against oil and e-commerce logistics facilities. Russia said it intercepted 351 drones overnight and reported civilian deaths.  
**Why it matters:** Kyiv is increasingly combining suppression of Russian air defenses with attacks on military and economic infrastructure. The growing scale and widening target set increase pressure on Russia but also raise the risk of civilian casualties and retaliation.

### 3. European leaders rally around Kyiv, but peace efforts remain stalled
Leaders from Britain, the EU and several European states met in Kyiv under the Coalition of the Willing framework. They pledged continued support and discussed air defense and pressure on Moscow. Reporting indicates no substantive progress in negotiations, with Russia and Ukraine remaining divided over territorial and political demands.  
**Why it matters:** Europe is assuming a larger role in sustaining Ukraine as relations between Kyiv and Washington cool and battlefield diplomacy remains frozen.

### 4. Syria and Israel resume US-mediated security talks
Syria’s foreign minister met an Israeli delegation reportedly led by the Mossad chief in Jordan. Talks covered mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks and arrests, revive negotiations on a security agreement, and prevent Israeli-Turkish tensions from spilling into Syria.  
**Why it matters:** The talks offer a possible channel for containing escalation after Israeli strikes in Syria, but major disagreements remain over Israeli withdrawals, Syrian military sovereignty and Turkish activity.

### 5. Iran-US economic confrontation produces regional military precautions
Iran warned that countries supporting Washington’s economic campaign could be treated as enemies. Greece reportedly moved a Patriot battery to Crete near Souda Bay, while Bulgaria relocated two US refueling aircraft after Iranian threats against US assets in southeastern Europe. Washington is preparing additional economic measures against Tehran.  
**Why it matters:** Economic pressure is increasingly intersecting with military deterrence, creating potential risks for US facilities, European allies and regional energy routes.

## WATCH

- **Ukraine’s winter air-defense gap:** Whether additional Patriot interceptors arrive before further Russian ballistic-missile attacks—and whether strikes on launchers can compensate for shortages.
- **Russian response to Ukraine’s expanding deep-strike campaign:** Potential retaliation against Ukrainian economic infrastructure and further increases in civilian casualties on both sides.
- **Syria-Israel negotiations:** Prospects for a security mechanism, especially regarding Israeli withdrawal demands, Turkish deployments and the Golan Heights.

## Taiwan Plans Large-Scale Live-Fire Naval Exercise

Taiwan’s navy will conduct drills from 9–24 September in three warning zones off the island’s southeastern coast. The exercise will include live fire against maritime and aerial targets and involve fighter aircraft, helicopters and reconnaissance drones.

**Why it matters:** The drills will test joint maritime and air capabilities in waters increasingly affected by Chinese military and coast guard activity. Their location also highlights Taiwan’s focus on defending its eastern approaches, traditionally considered less exposed than the Taiwan Strait.

## Chinese Activity Expands East of Taiwan

Chinese military and coast guard operations near Taiwan’s eastern waters have increased. Recent activity included Chinese navigation exercises with an Indonesian frigate, coast guard deployments near Lanyu, and what a Taiwanese official described as a record presence of more than 110 Chinese military and coast guard vessels along the First Island Chain.

**Why it matters:** A sustained Chinese presence east of Taiwan could increase pressure on the island beyond the Taiwan Strait and complicate Taiwan’s maritime surveillance and defense planning. Chinese exercises with regional partners also carry diplomatic significance as Beijing seeks broader operational engagement.

## Amnesty Alleges Unlawful Force Against Indian Protesters

Amnesty International said verified imagery and witness testimony showed Indian police and paramilitary personnel using pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas, grenades, batons and electric-shock devices during CJP-led protests in Delhi and Bihar from 20–24 July. It also documented two alleged instances of unlawful lethal force and said no Delhi officer had been held accountable one month later. Delhi Police denied disproportionate force.

**Why it matters:** The findings raise concerns about police accountability, civil liberties and the handling of political demonstrations in India. Continued impunity could heighten domestic tensions and attract further legal and international scrutiny.

## WATCH

- The weapons, scale and operational scenarios used in Taiwan’s September exercise, as well as any Chinese military response.
- Whether Indian authorities open independent investigations or pursue accountability over the protest policing allegations.

## 1. Europe expands military support as Ukraine’s air defences run low

**What happened:** European leaders met in Kyiv under the Coalition of the Willing. The European Commission approved an additional €6.1 billion for Ukrainian air and missile defence systems, interceptors, ammunition and radars. Britain also authorized the release of classified information on British components in SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles, supporting proposed French-Ukrainian production in Ukraine.

**Why it matters:** Ukraine faces intensified Russian ballistic-missile attacks and a shortage of Patriot interceptors. The measures could strengthen both its near-term air defence and its longer-term ability to produce deep-strike weapons domestically, while demonstrating continued European support amid stalled diplomacy.

## 2. Ukraine targets Russian launchers, aircraft and air-defence networks

**What happened:** President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had begun operations to locate and strike Russian ballistic-missile launchers near the border, including a reported strike on an Iskander launcher. Ukrainian commanders also reported drone attacks against Russian Su-33 and MiG-29 fighters, an Orion drone, S-400 and other air-defence systems, and multiple radars in southern Russia and occupied Crimea.

**Why it matters:** Striking launchers before they fire offers Ukraine an alternative to intercepting ballistic missiles, for which it has limited ammunition. Attacks on aircraft, radars and air-defence systems could also weaken Russia’s ability to conduct and defend against long-range operations, although the reported damage has not been independently verified.

## 3. Ukrainian deep strikes broaden to Russian economic logistics

**What happened:** Ukraine intensified drone attacks inside Russia, targeting oil infrastructure and logistics centers belonging to major e-commerce companies Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv says these networks support Russian military supply chains. Russian authorities and companies reported warehouse fires, evacuations and civilian casualties; Ozon shares also fell following the attacks.

**Why it matters:** The campaign seeks to raise the economic cost of the war, disrupt logistics and reduce the Russian rear’s insulation from the conflict. Its expansion toward dual-use commercial infrastructure increases risks to civilians and could prompt stronger Russian retaliation against Ukrainian economic and energy targets.

## WATCH

- **German long-range strike plans:** Berlin is considering nearly €12 billion for cruise missiles, U.S. Typhon launchers and future British-German systems, but the funding still requires parliamentary approval.
- **Russia–UK relations:** Moscow has withdrawn its ambassador without naming a replacement and warned of consequences over British support for Ukrainian strikes, raising the possibility of a further diplomatic downgrade.

### 1. US-Iran Economic Confrontation Escalates

**What happened:** The United States is preparing a major new sanctions package against Iran, potentially targeting Iranian oil buyers, financial intermediaries and Chinese refineries. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that countries supporting the campaign could be treated as hostile and said Iran could disrupt Gulf oil exports. President Masoud Pezeshkian nevertheless described the previous US-Iran memorandum as the best route back to negotiations.

**Why it matters:** Further sanctions and Iranian retaliation could intensify pressure on Iran’s economy, complicate US-China relations and disrupt energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The competing messages from Tehran also indicate tension between diplomatic engagement and coercive deterrence.

### 2. Syria and Israel Resume US-Mediated Security Talks

**What happened:** Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani met a high-level Israeli delegation, reportedly led by Mossad chief Roman Gofman, in Jordan. The talks addressed halting Israeli strikes and arrests, restoring the 1974 disengagement framework and preventing Israel-Turkey tensions from spilling into Syria. Damascus rejected limits on rebuilding its military or choosing foreign partners.

**Why it matters:** The meeting reopens a diplomatic channel after Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase over an alleged planned Turkish deployment. A security arrangement could reduce the risk of direct Israeli-Syrian escalation, but disagreements over Israeli withdrawals, Syrian sovereignty and Turkey’s military role remain substantial.

### 3. Iranian Threats Prompt Defensive Moves in Southeastern Europe

**What happened:** Greece reportedly moved a Patriot air-defence battery to Crete to protect the strategically important Souda Bay area following Iranian threats against US facilities in Europe. Bulgaria confirmed that two US KC-135 refuelling aircraft had left Bezmer Air Base after Tehran warned that countries supporting US operations could face consequences.

**Why it matters:** The moves show that the US-Iran confrontation is affecting NATO’s southeastern flank and forcing European governments to reassess the vulnerability of US military infrastructure. They also raise questions about alliance air-defence capacity against long-range missiles and drones.

### WATCH

- **Strait of Hormuz:** Iran-Oman talks on managing maritime traffic, alongside the new US sanctions announcement, could determine whether shipping disruption worsens.
- **Red Sea security:** An unidentified projectile struck a vessel west of Yanbu, Saudi Arabia, amid continuing Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping.

### 1. U.S. Navy unveils ultra-long-range air-to-air missile

The Navy displayed Raytheon’s AIM-424 Malice on F-35C and F/A-18E carrier-based fighters. The missile reportedly has a range exceeding 463 km, while the F-35C can carry it internally. Its integration status and intended operational role remain unclear.

**Why it matters:** If fielded as described, the missile could substantially extend carrier aviation’s engagement range and improve its ability to threaten high-value aircraft while keeping launch platforms farther from enemy defenses. It may complement or partially replace the Navy’s AIM-174.

### 2. Navy advances lower-cost long-range strike weapons

The Navy awarded two contracts under its CHAOS program, reportedly involving CoAspire’s RAACM-ER and Zone 5 Technologies’ Rusty Dagger. The project seeks scalable, precision-guided weapons for land and maritime targets, initially using ground launchers and later ships or aircraft. Mass production is expected from 2028.

**Why it matters:** The program is intended to expand U.S. and allied long-range strike capacity, address anti-ship missile shortages and reduce reliance on more expensive munitions. Shipboard adaptation could increase the number and geographic reach of available strike platforms.

### 3. Immigration enforcement increasingly affects military families

U.S. authorities detained Luis Manuel Aviles, the Nicaraguan father of an active-duty sailor, while seeking his deportation. The Associated Press reported that dozens of relatives of active-duty personnel have been detained as the Trump administration narrows immigration protections, with at least six deported.

**Why it matters:** Enforcement against military families could affect service-member morale, retention and readiness, particularly during prolonged deployments. It also signals that military family connections will not generally exempt undocumented relatives from the administration’s deportation policy.

## WATCH

- **Missile integration and procurement:** Monitor testing, production decisions and confirmed operational roles for the AIM-424 and CHAOS weapons.
- **Military-family immigration protections:** Watch for policy changes, court challenges and evidence of broader effects on personnel readiness and retention.

Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' —Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Key developments on Aug. 22-23:
- 'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
- Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says
- Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
- Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
- Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system, with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.

 Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says 
Ukraine is preparing changes to its mobilization system, including potential revisions to the country's draft age, secretary of the parliamentary defense committee Roman Kostenko said on Aug. 22.
Kostenko said that financial incentives offered to encourage Ukrainians to sign military contracts have failed to significantly increase recruitment, prompting officials to consider other measures.
"There are already talks and, as far as I know, some things are changing in the draft age," Kostenko said, adding that the Defense Ministry or General Staff would provide further details. He declined to say whether the draft age could be lowered or raised.
The lawmaker noted that Ukraine does not plan to move away from compulsory mobilization in favor of an exclusively voluntary system.
Kostenko also denied reports that authorities are considering eliminating mobilization exemptions for parents with three or more children, saying there are no such legislative initiatives currently under consideration.
No changes are planned regarding the mobilization of women, Kostenko said, adding that military service for women will remain voluntary.
As the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine goes on, mobilization has become among the most contentious domestic issues in the country.
Ukraine's military faces a growing need to replenish fighting units, build reserves, and allow existing soldiers to rotate off the front line. As Ukraine steps up its mobilization efforts, draft offices are often accused of forced conscription without compliance with fundamental civil rights and ill-treatment of conscripts.
Under martial law, Ukrainian men aged 25 to 60 are currently subject to conscription and are forbidden from leaving the country except under a certain number of specific circumstances.
Meanwhile, Russia reportedly plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Aug. 23.

Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
Ukraine's military reportedly launched a drone attack on the Russian city of Orenburg overnight on Aug. 23, striking an Ozon logistics center, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Photos and videos posted to social media purport to show smoke rising from the warehouse following a reported strike. Air raid alerts were active in the region ahead of the reported strike.
The attack on Ozon, Russia's second-largest online marketplace and main competitor to Wildberries, marked the second reported strike on the company's facilities. The first direct attack on the company's logistics centers occurred just one night earlier on Aug. 22 in a Ukrainian attack on Samara Oblast.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
The full extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
After months of strikes on Wildberries facilities, Ukraine’s military appears to have shifted its focus to Ozon sites across Russia, with Ukrainian officials justifying the attacks on the grounds that the company sells goods to the Russian military.
"Systematic strikes on storage centers for dual-use goods are making it more difficult for the enemy to operate and are negatively impacting the overall economy of Russia," the Defense Ministry said after the Aug. 22 attack.
Orenburg is located in southwestern Russia near the border to Kazakhstan, approximately 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russia-Ukraine border.
Elsewhere in Russia, a massive blaze erupted at a warehouse in St. Petersburg overnight on Aug. 22, officials reported.
Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry said the first spread to engulf an area of at least 82,000 square metres (approximately 882,000 square feet) in the Kolpino district, southeast of central St. Petersburg.
The fire, located in an industrial part of the city, reportedly burned adjacent to an Ozon logistics center, owned by Russia's second-largest online marketplace and the main competitor to Wildberries.
The cause of the blaze was not immediately clear. Air raid alerts had not been declared in the Leningrad Oblast, nor were explosions heard in the area.

Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."

Ukrainian drones have struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said on Aug. 23.
The two jets, a Su-33 and a Mig-29, as well as a large Orion strike drone, were hit at the Vityazevo airfield in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar Krai, Brovdi said.
The Orion is a large Russian unmanned aerial vehicle developed by Russia before the full-scale invasion and similar in class to the Turkish-made Bayraktar TB-2 operated by Ukraine.

Over 2026, Russia adapted the Orion for a new role: launching the cheap Banderol cruise missile, now regularly used against Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine 35 Years Old – The Ukrainian Army Has Become Europe’s Most Powerful
articles.body:
When Russia first tried to steal Ukraine’s Donbas region by sending soldiers and armed gangs to take over government buildings and hold gunpoint elections, there was little that the Ukrainian military could do but send a few poorly paid, ill equipped and weakly manned army units.
It was a bad time to be a Ukrainian soldier. Salaries were unpaid, theft of army supplies was rampant, and in a good year only about one in ten of the country’s combat brigades actually could take the field. In those days a Kyiv waitress earned more than a line officer.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Things were so bad in Mariupol on May 9, 2014, that one junior Ukrainian mechanized infantry officer, confronted by separatist crowds and barricades blocking his tiny column from driving to the local city hall, had zero air power, artillery, support units or even tanks or mortars behind him. No one knew about drones. His chain of command didn’t seem to want to help. As the incident played out, that young Ukrainian army Major aged 31 decided he had few options but to order his driver to ram a BMP fighting vehicle into the roadblock at full speed. Russian content creators had been on hand and hoped to record government troops firing at “peaceful” civilians but there was no content.
The Mariupol mayor’s office returned to government control and remained Ukrainian until Russia invaded a second time, in 2022. When that happened, most of Ukraine’s neighbors and allies said the Kremlin would demolish the Ukrainian army in days.
UK Allows Release of Storm Shadow Missile Data to Boost Ukraine Production
Now that once obscure Ukrainian officer, Major General Mykhailo Drapaty, is the supreme commander of the biggest and by many measures most technologically advanced army in Europe: the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
In 1991 the AFU was a shadow and Ukraine’s territory was a textbook undefended vacuum into which the Kremlin hard and soft power could only expand.
In two decades of hybrid warfare and more than a decade of open warfare, the Kremlin has tried to destroy the AFU. But it hasn’t worked. Instead of eliminating resistance in Ukraine, Russian hybrid war and conventional war assault have created a battle-tested armed adversary whose sole purpose is destroying Russian soldiers and military equipment as efficiently as possible. They have become extremely good at it and they are improving daily.As Ukraine celebrates its 35th year of independence, the Kremlin is reckoning with a war-hardened enemy that is more agile and more ruthlessly able to find and exploit Russian weak points than any adversary faced by Russia in two centuries, at least. Unlike in peacetime NATO, Ukraine’s armed forces aren’t just hoping to be prepared to fight a modern war. They are serious about being able to fight.
More than anyone, the Ukrainian people are fully convinced that the only way to contain Russian aggression is to field an army able not just to stop Russia’s armed forces, but to make the Kremlin regret attacking in the first place. The catalogue of Ukrainian military advances driven equally by the basic instinct of self-defense and often peculiar “allied” strings on certain weapons donated to Ukraine, and even more by the US’ wholesale halt to entire arms assistance packages, is dizzying.
Ukraine has become the free world’s most prolific howitzer manufacturer with the 155mm Bohdana, its Neptune cruise missiles have sunk the Russian Black Sea Fleet’s biggest warship (and flagship), and waves of sleek missile-drones, stubby pusher-prop drones, along with proper cruise missiles and long-winged deep reconnaissance robot spy planes, all of it domestically-developed, wing their way into Russia, usually 300+ aircraft nightly.
For years the Kremlin has asserted its national air defense network was the world’s most effective. Ukraine’s drone swarms say something different.
In July 2026 alone, Ukrainian drones struck more than 200+ shadow fleet tankers and other ships and 1,000+ cargo trucks. According to Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces – a branch of service invented by the AFU – every three months Ukrainian tactical drones eliminate about 7-80,000 Russian soldiers and about 3-5,00 Russian combat vehicles, or a force bigger than the British army.
In the AFU, AI-assisted drone targeting was experimental six months ago. Now the tech is standard for strike packages beyond 30 km (19 miles) from the front.
AFU thinking is: Modern war is fought with drones.
In 2025, factories and volunteers reportedly delivered four million drones to the troops and in 2026 the figure appears on track to reach seven million. Europe’s two most prolific drone manufacturers, Croatia and Turkey, likely together manufacture around 400-500,000 drones annually. The US output is probably half that.
Ukrainian military software engineers, in the old days many hackers and computer gamers, have revolutionized military data flows and pushed apps down to the soldier level so that any fighter with a smart phone (and the right access) can see every single spotted Russian tank and soldier on the ground. This also includes any drone or missile seen by the country’s air defense network in the sky, at the punch of a few buttons.
In 2023-24, Ukraine’s allies warned that their own armies lacked proper radars and fighter jets and interceptor missiles to counter swarms of cheap Russian Shahed drones attacking Ukraine. Creating an air defense network unlike any other on Earth, the Ukrainians mounted thousands of acoustic sensors across the country, data-linked them together, and built the software that analyzed the digital acoustic data to compute the Russian drone was and where it was flying – all in real time.
On July 30, a single Russian cruise missile either wayward or intended to test NATO air defenses flew about 60 miles into Poland, was not intercepted, and blew up in a farm field. That same night Ukrainian air defenses claimed that of 61 Russian cruise missiles violating Ukrainian air space, its forces shot down 53. Some of the Ukrainian shoot downs were by 30-year-old F-16s cast off by NATO air forces as too old for modern war.
The bottom line? Thanks to lucrative energy exports to the West, the Kremlin in the 2000s reasserted control over the Russian people and economy and poured resources into rearmament.
The US and Europe initially mostly ignored growing Russian military power, then dismissed it as too weak to worry NATO, and later NATO states seemed to conclude Russian military power was too strong to oppose. Better to sacrifice countries like Georgia and Ukraine than confront Russia seriously.
The AFU’s fighting men and women have turned those calculations upside down. Where Russia previously once faced no substantial military obstacle between itself and NATO, there now is a large, technologically adaptive and battle-hardened one million man army not just able to interfere, but actively working hard day and night to invent new ways to harm Russian military capacity, even beyond the Urals.
Worse for Russia, Ukraine’s armed forces are backed by a Ukrainian nation with very few exceptions convinced freedom must be fought for and that appeasing Russia only encourages Russian military aggression.
For Ukraine’s neighbors and allies, the metamorphasis of the AFU from an organization unable to find fuel for its tanks, into a force fully capable of fighting the armed forces of the Russian Federation to a standstill, is geopolitical earthquake.
For Russia, ironically, the rise of the AFU and Ukrainian armed forces arguably achieved one of Vladimir Putin’s 2022 war aims – sideline NATO from European security and split up the alliance if possible. Just not the way he intended.
From the point of view of a Kremlin looking to expand westwards in accordance with classic Russian geopolitical strategy, NATO has indeed, finally, more than three decades after the break-up of the Soviet Union, been at least marginalized. But even if NATO failed to deter Russia in the past and can’t decide what to about Russia now, Ukraine at 35 years old is no longer a soft target.
Instead, between Russia and Europe, stand the men and bayonets of the AFU: the most combat-capable and lethal army on the European continent.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
articles.body:
A screenshot from a video of a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian Su-33 fighter jet at Vityazevo air base in Krasnodar Krai, Russia. (Robert Brovdi / Telegram)
Ukrainian drones have struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said on Aug. 23.
The two jets, a Su-33 and a Mig-29, as well as a large Orion strike drone, were hit at the Vityazevo airfield in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar Krai, Brovdi said.
The Orion is a large Russian unmanned aerial vehicle developed by Russia before the full-scale invasion and similar in class to the Turkish-made Bayraktar TB-2 operated by Ukraine.
On a battlefield dense with enemy air defense assets and interceptor drones on both sides, drones the Orion and TB-2 have been largely rendered useless.
Over 2026, Russia adapted the Orion for a new role: launching the cheap Banderol cruise missile, now regularly used against Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure.
All three strikes, videos of which were shared on Brovdi's Telegram channel, were carried out by the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, which specializes in long-range strikes.
Other targets included S-400, Pantsir, and Tor air defense systems, as well as eight high-value radars in Krasnodar Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Russian-occupied Crimea.
Francis Farrell is a senior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is the co-author of War Notes, the Kyiv Independent's weekly newsletter about the war. For the second year in a row, the Kyiv Independent received a grant from the Charles Douglas-Home Memorial Trust to support his front-line reporting for the year 2025-2026. Francis won the Prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandy for war correspondents in the young reporter category in 2023, and was nominated for the European Press Prize in 2024.
Francis speaks Ukrainian and Hungarian and is an alumnus of Leiden University in The Hague and University College London. He has previously worked as a managing editor at the online media project Lossi 36, as a freelance journalist and documentary photographer, and at the OSCE and Council of Europe field missions in Albania and Ukraine.

articles.title: Burnham and European leaders arrive in Kyiv as Ukraine marks Independence Day
articles.body:
European leaders join Zelenskyy in Kyiv for Ukraine’s Independence Day as Russian invasion pushes on
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — European leaders joined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday for official celebrations marking Ukraine’s Independence Day as Russia pushes on with its 4-year-old invasion of the country.
One of President Vladimir Putin’s key goals in starting a war with Russia’s neighbor in February 2022 was to place Kyiv in Moscow’s orbit. Ukrainians voted overwhelmingly for independence in 1991.
With no significant changes on the front line for months and no apparent progress after more than a year of U.S.-led peace efforts, the warring countries are locked in a spiral of escalating aerial attacks that are killing civilians and smashing infrastructure.
EU leaders rally around Ukraine
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, on his first overseas trip since taking office last month, on Monday joined almost a dozen other European leaders, as well as other dignitaries including European Council President Antonio Costa, in Kyiv.
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side.”
Burnham was to co-chair a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing group of countries helping Ukraine resist Russia’s onslaught, with the leaders of France and Germany expected to join online.
The visiting leaders took to Kyiv pledges of further military and financial support. Burnham is expected to announce that the U.K. Government has agreed to allow defense company MBDA to release classified information relating to British components used in the SCALP long-range missile, according to his office. That would pave the way for France and Ukraine to advance plans for local production of the weapon in Ukraine.
SCALP is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared French and British technology.
Ukraine has leaned heavily on NATO countries for help fighting Russia’s bigger army, although relations with the United States have been cooler under President Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, is getting help from North Korea and China.
Both Russia and Ukraine are trying through long-range strikes to inflict economic pain, disrupt military supplies and erode public morale.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have repeatedly hit facilities in Russia’s vital oil industry, causing fuel shortages, and have also engaged in a campaign against Russia’s largest online retailer Wildberries.
Ukrainian strikes kill 3 teenagers
Three teenagers were killed and six children were wounded in the southern Russian city of Krasnodar, Russia’s children’s rights ombudswoman Maria Lvova-Belova said Monday, as Ukraine attacked several warehouses of Ozon for the third straight day, according to officials and the company.
Ozon is one of Russia’s major e-commerce retailers. The company said a large fire raged at an Ozon logistics facility in the suburbs of Krasnodar following the overnight attack.
A drone also hit the grounds of an Ozon logistics center in the southern Russian region of Adygeya, regional governor Murat Kumpilov said, though the company said its Adygeya warehouse wasn’t damaged.
In all, four Ozon premises appeared to have been targeted.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted and destroyed 351 Ukrainian drones over eight Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the waters of the Azov and the Black Seas.
The ministry also said that its forces overnight continued to strike Ukrainian ports and vessels delivering cargo for the armed forces.

articles.body:
This live page is now closed.

•    Two people have been killed in Gaza in fresh Israeli airstrikes targeting the centre of the strip.
•    Israel conducted new airstrikes near Nabatieh in south Lebanon overnight.
•    Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is starting a two-day visit to France.

Lebanon's state media NNA reports Israeli airstrikes and artillery shelling on Nabatiyeh El Faouqa and Kfar Roummane in southern Lebanon.
Sudan's armed forces claim to have destroyed a Rapid Support Forces convoy in the country's Blue Nile State, killing four personnel killed, including a major.
An Israeli strike targeted a tent sheltering displaced people south of Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah, Gaza, according to Palestinian media.
At least two people were killed and several other civilians were injured.
Armed groups from the "National Guard" militia affiliated with the Druze Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri blocked the Damascus-Sweida road on Sunday, at the um al-Zaytoun checkpoint in the northern countryside of Sweida governorate, preventing civilians from heading towards the capital, before reopening the road later.

Israeli forces have released a Syrian citizen who was kidnapped during an incursion in the town of Al-Rafid in the southern countryside of Quneitra governorate in southwestern Syria, while he was grazing sheep west of the town.
The troops set up a temporary checkpoint in the village of um Al-Azam in the central countryside of the governorate, during which they searched passers-by in the evening.
The US special envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey on Sunday walked back his comments from two days ago that Israel "still" occupies the Golan Heights in violation of UN resolutions, remarks that went against US President Donald Trump 's position on the Syrian territory.
Ambassador Tom Barrack on Friday said that Israel "still" occupies the territory in an interview with Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal.
Barrack now says that was a description of the territory’s historical status, "not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position" on the Golan.

Kuwait's emir on Sunday approved a decree banning naturalised citizens from voting, two years after dissolving parliament and embarking on a mass nationality stripping campaign.
Previously, naturalised Kuwaitis were able to vote 30 years after acquiring the nationality, but were banned from running for office or being appointed.
Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah issued a decree "amending certain provisions of the Kuwaiti Nationality Law", Kuwait's official KUNA news agency reported.
Iraq has deployed three army brigades along its border with Saudi Arabia under a newly established Desert Operations Command, seeking to stop militias from using Iraqi territory to launch attacks against the kingdom, senior military officials told The New Arab.
The move follows drone attacks on Saudi energy facilities in late July, which Riyadh and Washington said were launched from Iraq by Iran-aligned armed groups. The factions have denied responsibility.
The force, led by Major General Imad Ubaid al-Maliki, has been deployed across the Al-Salman, Basiyah, and Shabaka areas in the Najaf desert, where its aim is to secure desert roads and routes leading to the Jumaimah border crossing, backed by Iraqi reconnaissance aircraft.

Israel warned Hamas it would intensify strikes in Gaza and order civilians to evacuate areas if the launching of drones, balloons and kites from the Gaza Strip toward Israel does not stop immediately, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said in a statement on Sunday.

Israeli media said that a 16-year-old was arrested.

Iran has discovered over 7.5 trillion cubic feet of gas in a field south of its Fars Province, Iran's oil minister Mohsen Paknejad said in comments carried by state media on Sunday.

"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn’t bring results, then we don’t need it," Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
Washington has been trying to broker a security pact between President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government and Israel, which has occupied swathes of southern Syria and repeatedly bombed the country following the overthrow of the Assad regime.
He said that around the beginning of the year, the sides had "agreed on paper to almost everything" regarding a security deal that would require Israel to stop attacking Syria and was tied to its withdrawal from territory seized after Assad fell.

Medics are treating the 24-year-old man for his injuries while Israeli troops are searching for the attacker.
Residents of Al-Auja were forced to abandon the village earlier this year under threat from constant settler attacks.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended a recent memorandum of understanding as the best way for the country to move beyond what he described as a situation of "neither war nor peace".
In a speech published by state-run IRNA on Sunday, he said members of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council believed the memorandum represented the best possible agreement based on what he described as dignity, wisdom and the national interest.
"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."
The deal signed by the two countries in June set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war and reaching an accord on its nuclear program. That period ended last week, but the two sides remain far apart, with no signs of compromise on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Pakistan's powerful army chief Asim Munir will visit Tehran on Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday.
Baghaei said the visit was in continuation of Pakistan's efforts to strengthen peace and security in the region.
Pakistan has led international efforts to broker a peace deal between Iran and the US.
Lebanon's state-run news agency is reporting that Israel carried out a new round of airstrikes and shelling around the Ali al-Taher ridge, east of Nabatieh in south Lebanon.
Israel claims that a major Hezbollah base is located under the ridge and has been attempting to seize the control of the area. 
Iran on Sunday executed a man convicted of acting as an agent of Israel and the United States during January anti-government protests.
The judiciary said Majid Adineh had been convicted of "operational action in favour of hostile groups" in nationwide rallies that broke out late last year.
Adineh is one of a string of people put to death over the protests, which were sparked by economic hardships in Iran.
He was accused of "deliberate arson, gathering and collusion with the intention of committing crimes against the country's internal security", the judiciary's Mizan Online website said in a report Sunday.
"Based on numerous documents and evidence in the case and the defendant's statements, the Karaj Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death and confiscation of all his property."
An appeal by Adineh was unsuccessful and the Supreme Court upheld the verdict, with his execution carried out Sunday morning, Mizan said.
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' economic war against the Islamic Republic, saying they would be considered enemies.
Washington has pushed its allies to back its new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy, as the President Trump's unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark.
"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's supreme national security council, on state television.
"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.
If the countries concerned refused to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.
Rezaei also said that the Islamic Republic had more cards to play in the war, claiming that "we have not yet attacked any American economic interests".
"So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them," he said.
Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake", he added.

articles.title: Live: Ukraine backers gather as Russian attacks escalate, air defence runs low
articles.body:
Live: Ukraine backers gather as Russian missile attacks escalate and air defences run low
Ukraine on Monday hosts a meeting of its key European backers to press for air-defence supplies and more pressure on Moscow, with Russian attacks killing more civilians than at any time since the first months of the invasion. The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Two killed in Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Belgorod region, authorities say
Two people were killed and two more injured in Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia's Belgorod region, the region's government said in a post on Telegram.
Zelensky, on Ukraine's independence day, says Ukraine wants peace but 'will not just give in'
Germany's Wadephul to urge Rubio to take more active role on Ukraine
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul plans to speak to his US counterpart, Marco Rubio, by phone to urge him to become more personally involved in diplomatic efforts related to the war in Ukraine, he told radio broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.
Wadephul, who was recently in Ukraine, told the broadcaster that US diplomacy had so far been handled largely by presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
"I may be able to encourage him (Rubio) myself to do more there," the German minister said, adding that Berlin was pursuing other channels to help restart negotiations.
Ukraine hit Russian fighter aircraft, two vessels in Black Sea
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian MIG-29 fighter aircraft and two Russian vessels in Black Sea overnight, Ukraine's drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said.
Brovdi said on the Telegram app that one of the vessels attacked was a tanker, and the other was a bulk carrier.
EU approves further €6.1 billion for Ukraine's defence
The European Commission approved a further €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in financial aid for Ukraine to procure new defence systems, such as air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.
The EU said this latest aid package came on top of €16 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion had already been disbursed.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a statement.
EU's Costa, UK's Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day
European Council President Antonio Costa and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv to mark the country's independence day, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
The visiting dignitaries also included Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldova's President Maia Sandu and Estonia's President Alar Karis, Sybiha said on X, posting photos of the officials arriving at the Kyiv station.
Russia downs 351 Ukrainian drones overnight, defence ministry says
The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces had intercepted and destroyed 351 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions.
Russia says its forces hit tanker carrying fuel near Ukraine's Odesa
The Russian Defence Ministry said it had hit a tanker carrying fuel and lubricants for Ukrainian troops in the port of Pivdennyi near Odesa, as well as port infrastructure facilities used for unloading and storing military cargo.
Zelensky rejects rival's call for elections
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has rejected the prospect of wartime elections, saying it would be highly dangerous.
Analysis by FRANCE 24 international affairs editor Matthew-Mary Caruchet.
Ukraine keeps up attacks on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon
Russian e-commerce giant Ozon said that its warehouses came under drone attack, as Ukraine pressed ahead with its campaign targeting logistics sites.
Kyiv has for weeks mounted a campaign targeting Russia's Wildberries – the country's top online retailer – alleging it supplied components to the military.
Ozon is Russia's second-largest online marketplace, with its pick-up points and delivery boxes ubiquitous across the country.
New UK PM Andy Burnham to make visit to Kyiv
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Kyiv on his first international visit since taking office last month, his office said, as Ukraine marks its 35th independence anniversary.
Burnham has vowed to give strong support to Ukraine as it battles Russia's invasion.
The Labour Party leader's visit comes as he announced that Britain had "agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine", a statement said.
Zelensky says war time elections in Ukraine would 'destroy the country'
In remarks on Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke out against holding war time elections, saying it would be too dangerous for the country and would "split" Ukraine.
The remarks come in response to a call from the former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov to organise a vote, after he was fired by Zelensky last month.
Details and analysis by FRANCE 24 correspondent in Kyiv, Emmanuelle Chaze.
Russia's Ozon says Dagestan logistics hub on fire after drone attack
Russian online retailer Ozon's logistics hub in Makhachkala in Dagestan was on fire after a drone attack, it said on the Telegram messaging app.
The company has also temporarily shut down two warehouses in the nearby regions of Stavropol and Adygeya in the North Caucasus amid a drone attack alert, it said, though they were not damaged.
North Korea preparing further Russia troop deployments, no sign move imminent, Seoul says
South Korea's Defence Ministry said North Korea was continuing preparations for an additional troop deployment to Russia, but had detected no signs that such a deployment was imminent, according to a South Korean lawmaker's office.
The assessment came after North Korea's Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, last week denied Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's claim that Pyongyang planned to send up to 50,000 more troops to Russia to fight for its ally.
South Korea's Defence Ministry said in a statement to lawmaker Yu Yong-weon that North Korea had continued to supply Russia with weapons systems, including short-range ballistic missiles, according to Yu's office.
Drone debris kills two children in Russia's Krasnodar, governor says
Two children were killed and another nine people, including seven children, were injured after drone debris hit a private childcare center in Krasnodar in southern Russia overnight, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on the Telegram messaging app.
Debris also fell on apartment buildings in the city, causing a fire at warehouses, he said, without providing details.

articles.title: Germany Plans €12 Billion Long-Range Arsenal to Deter Russia
articles.body:
The German government plans to invest approximately €12 billion ($14 billion) to develop a new arsenal of long-range weapons aimed at deterring Russia, Politico reported.
The initiative, described in the documents as a key priority for both Germany and NATO, aims to equip the German armed forces with the ability to strike targets hundreds or thousands of kilometers behind enemy lines.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The conventional, “below the nuclear threshold” capabilities would be used to target command posts, airfields, missile launchers, and supply hubs.
The ministry’s strategy consists of a four-part plan. The first phase involves deploying a new, low-cost cruise missile starting in 2027. The second phase focuses on the United States, with an internal goal to achieve initial operational readiness of US Typhon launchers armed with Tomahawk missiles by the end of the decade, providing Berlin with a proven interim weapon.
The final two phases of the plan involve the joint development of highly advanced weapon systems with the United Kingdom, slated for introduction by the middle of the next decade.
According to the internal documents, the capacity building will require “nearly €12 billion” in state funds. The funding has not yet been approved but was submitted as part of the state budget planning process.
A spokesperson for the German Defense Ministry declined to comment to Politico on the specific figures or individual programs, stating that the ministry will only comment after parliamentary review.
Lithuanian President Nausėda Arrives in Kyiv Ahead of Independence Day
“The measures you are talking about are generally subject to approval by the German Bundestag,” the spokesperson said.
Russian hybrid threats in Germany
The military buildup comes as Germany weighs taking diplomatic action against Moscow over mounting hybrid security threats.
The German government is currently reviewing the international legal basis for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and has not ruled out terminating a 2011 bilateral agreement that allows it to operate. Germany’s next opportunity to terminate the agreement takes effect in June 2027, requiring Berlin to notify Moscow by Dec. 6, 2026.
The Foreign Ministry cited “Russia’s increasing hybrid activities” as the primary reason for the review. The Russian House, operated by the sanctioned Russian state agency Rossotrudnichestvo, has traditionally hosted cultural events but is now facing heightened scrutiny.
The debate over the cultural center follows a recent incident where an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at the Leipzig/Halle Airport.
German federal prosecutors have taken over the investigation into the drone. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt characterized the incident as a potential “hybrid attack scenario” involving a foreign power, warning that Germany has become a daily target for espionage, sabotage, and cyberattacks.

articles.title: Flamingo missiles should become mass-produced "birds" and "winter" in Russia – Zelenskyy's address
articles.body:
Flamingo missiles should become mass-produced "birds" and "winter" in Russia – Zelenskyy's address
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has highlighted the key role of Ukraine's defence industry in defending the country's independence and expressed hope that Ukraine's domestically produced Flamingo missiles will play an important role in the winter military confrontation with Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy's address to Ukrainians on the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence
Quote: "Our defence industry today is truly a giant, forging independence 24/7. And we have to do more. Tens of thousands of ground robotic systems are carrying out extremely dangerous missions at the front and have already saved thousands of soldiers. But we have to do more. Our naval drones are in action: the enemy had a fleet, and it is becoming scrap. But we have to sink more.
Our mid-range strikes are cutting their logistics. Our long-range capabilities are cutting their profits. Thousands of our deep strikes have already been seen in Moscow, Tuapse, Tula, Ryazan, Olenya, Omsk, and dozens more places where our Ukrainian justice has already reached. Russia must see more of this justice. Flamingos should not be a rare species but birds arriving en masse. They must 'winter' in Russia."
Details: Zelenskyy stressed the need to find solutions to counter Russia's ballistic terror.
He also said he believes that all contradictions and fears about Russia will disappear in the US.
"The Russians must be brought to the negotiating table. There finally must be sanctions that will make them howl. Ukraine must be given everything that will force them to end the war. And this is possible," the president said.
Quote: "We are not asking you to fight for us. Give Ukraine everything it needs to stop this war – to stop it faster than Putin can start the next one. To prevent that, we must act together. Europe must be Europe. United, ambitious, brave. China should no longer remain silent. When someone puts on a sailor's uniform and cap and, badly pronouncing some words, talks about a nuclear strike, China must respond, must cool their ardour. China must prove its ambition to be one of the world's leaders, not only economically and technologically but also as a civilisation – making it clear that no dictators have the right to threaten the planet with their old warheads."
Background:
- Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, says Russian leader Vladimir Putin does not want talks now and will be even less willing to negotiate once the cold weather arrives because he believes Ukrainians will not be able to survive the coming winter.
- Russia's Defence Ministry posted a photo of attack drones accompanied by a threat to "freeze" Ukraine this winter. The Strategic Communications Directorate of Ukraine's Armed Forces responded by promising to "keep warm by the fire of Russian oil refineries".

articles.title: Russia Withdraws Ambassador to UK as Tensions Rise over Britain’s Support for Ukraine
articles.body:
The Kremlin has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK as it seeks to pressure Britain into reconsidering its support for Ukraine, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, visiting Kyiv on his first foreign trip, will hand over blueprints for Ukraine to produce its own long-range missiles.
Ambassador Andrey Kelin had been in post for more than seven years and is understood to have left on July 21. Russia has not put forward a replacement for Kelin, while it is understood that embassy staff do not know if or when a successor might be named. Russia’s online list of “senior diplomatic staff” in the UK now only includes Vasily A Tsyganov, chargé d’affaires at the embassy.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A spokesperson for the Russian embassy in the UK told British newspaper The Sunday Times that the Kremlin had concluded Kelin’s diplomatic mission on July 21. The Kremlin did not appear to have made any official statement at the time. The embassy spokesperson added that the former ambassador had made “considerable efforts to preserve contacts and channels of communication” with the UK but accused the British government of choosing a “path of confrontation” with Russia.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said: “This is a matter for the Russian ministry of foreign affairs. We have an ambassador and embassy in Moscow to engage and raise concerns with the Russian government. We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, which has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal and unprovoked invasion.”
Ukrainian Drones Strike 2 Russian Fighter Jets, S-400, Radars
Escalating tensions
Tensions between Russia and the UK have ratcheted up in recent days, with Moscow issuing a warning through its UK embassy, stating – without further definition – that there would be “consequences” after it emerged that Britain was supplying drone technology to Kyiv.
In a statement on Telegram on Aug 17, the Russian embassy in the UK accused Britain of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis” and that “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer.”
Kyiv has stepped up attacks on Moscow and other parts of Russia in recent weeks, with a military source confirming to the BBC that UK drones had been used in attacks on Russia that reportedly caused more than £35bn in economic damage.
John Foreman, a former British defence attaché in Moscow and Kyiv, views Kelin’s withdrawal as a signal of Moscow’s disinterest in maintaining bilateral relations with the UK. In a post on X, Foreman stated: “The embassy’s strident ‘consequences’ statement this week and the huge deterioration of bilateral relations since 2018 and especially since the start of the war make me wonder if Moscow will permanently downgrade the relationship this time, by default by not replacing him.”
Following The Sunday Times report, the Russian embassy released a broader public statement to other national outlets – including The Guardian and The Telegraph – to deny that it was formally downgrading diplomatic relations, while simultaneously blaming London for pushing a path of confrontation.
Incoming British Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently stated that the UK is “with Ukraine 100%” as President Volodymyr Zelensky became his first international visitor.
Speaking to reporters on Aug. 18 after Moscow threatened “consequences” over drone supplies, Burnham said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin... We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
Missile blueprints
The UK appears to remain unfazed by the diplomatic rift with Moscow, as Burnham makes Kyiv the destination of his first foreign trip on Monday – Ukraine’s Independence Day. He is set to announce that Britain has agreed to allow UK defense company MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French equivalent of the UK’s storm shadow.
The move follows the UK being the first to gift long-range strike weapons for defensive purposes to Ukraine in 2023 and will allow the French and Ukrainians to move forward with the Ukrainian assembly of the missile.
Burnham said: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes. I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.”

articles.title: Ukraine Backers Gather as War Escalates, Air Defense Runs Low
articles.body:
Ukraine hosts a meeting of its key European backers on Monday to press for critical air-defense supplies and more pressure on Moscow, with Russian attacks killing more civilians than at any time since the first months of the invasion.
The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be in Kyiv for his first international trip since taking office, and several other leaders are expected to join remotely.
EU Council President Antonio Costa is also due in Kyiv for the talks, which come amid the latest, deadly escalation of the war.
Russia has been pounding Kyiv with ballistic missiles in recent weeks, ripping open apartment blocks and killing dozens of citizens in the capital.
The escalating Russian strikes have pushed civilian deaths to their highest levels since the first months of Russia’s 2022 invasion.
After almost every attack – which sees tens of thousands hunker in the Kyiv metro system and many more in basements and other shelters across the city – Zelensky has issued public pleas for more air-defense support.
Ahead of the meeting, Ukraine has forged ahead with its campaign against Russia’s logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early Monday at its warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.
Independent Ukraine at 35: State-Building Under Immense Pressure
Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack killed two children and wounded nine others.
UK, French support
Ukraine celebrates Independence Day on Monday, which also marks exactly four-and-a-half years since Russia invaded on Feb. 24, 2022.
“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve,” Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kyiv.
“We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”
Diplomacy on ending the conflict – Europe’s largest since World War II – is effectively frozen.
Russia is demanding hardline territorial and political concessions that Kyiv has rejected as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack.
Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorizing defense firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile.
And on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
“It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression,” Macron wrote on X.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop.
Kyiv’s homegrown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems – chiefly, US Patriot interceptors – to protect its skies.
But due to shortfalls globally since the US launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed.
Ukraine’s missiles shortfall
Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” Zelensky said.
“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.
The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles during its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites – including oil refineries and retail warehouses.
The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.
Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshalling support to Ukraine as uncertainty persists over US commitments under Donald Trump.

articles.title: Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv
articles.body:
Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv
- Published
Andy Burnham is marking his first foreign visit as prime minister with a trip to Kyiv - and will hand over blueprints so Ukraine can build its own long-range missiles.
The prime minister will chair his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.
He is also set to accept an award on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine and to take part in independence day events.
Crucially for the war effort, he will announce his government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French equivalent of the UK's Storm Shadow.
Burnham will be reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people.
On Monday morning Burnham laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Ahead of his visit on Monday, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.
"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."
He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
It comes after Moscow warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.
Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.
The long-range Scalp missile weighs 1,300kg and is 16.7ft (5.10m) in length. It is capable of hitting targets around 150 miles into Russia - not as far as Ukraine's deep strike drone capability but it is a significant step in showing the willingness of international partners to share weapons technology.
The maker describes them as designed to hit pre-planned, stationary targets. It can be used day and night in all weather, and has advanced navigation systems.
MBDA adds that it is in service with the Royal Air Force, the French Air Force, Italian Air Force and has been used in Iraq, Syria and Libya.
Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles.
On Sunday, he said they have requested 360 of the missiles, but are "working with countries on additional options".
Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.
While the Scalp missile does not intercept enemy attacks like the Patriots, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast they were sharing its blueprints so Ukraine could "defend against this illegal invasion that's now killed so many people".
"It's not just the front lines, it's shopping centres, it's housing that's being targeted by Russia in their illegal war and that's why we have said and we will continue to make sure our actions follow it that we will support Ukraine for as long as it takes," he added.
Pollard said Ukraine is in need of a variety of weapons, which is why the UK is supplying other air defence assets to take down Russian cruise missiles, and counter-drone measures.
The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".
In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."
Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".
The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.
The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.
Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.
A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.
It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.
Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
