articles.title: Inside Turkey’s military machine: Tanks, drones and regional power
articles.body:
The growing tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have taken on added significance in recent days amid military activity in Syria, have raised anew a question that has become increasingly relevant for Israel's defense establishment in recent years: How powerful is the Turkish military? The answer begins with striking numbers, but certainly does not end there.
Turkey is not merely a major NATO member. It is a regional military power whose influence stretches from the Black and Aegean seas through Syria and Iraq to the Caucasus and North Africa. NATO itself described Turkey ahead of the alliance's summit in Ankara in July as the country with the "alliance's second-largest army," after the United States. Its location between Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as its control of the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits, gives that power even greater strategic significance.
According to Global Firepower data for 2026, which is based in part on estimates, Turkey has about 481,000 active-duty military personnel, 380,000 reservists and another 150,000 members of paramilitary forces. Combined, the three categories account for more than 1 million people. By the number of active-duty personnel, Turkey ranks 10th worldwide according to the index.
More than 2,280 tanks and nearly 100,000 vehicles
The ground force is the backbone of the Turkish military. According to Global Firepower, its arsenal includes about 2,284 tanks and roughly 98,000 vehicles of various types. Alongside them, Turkey maintains a large artillery force: more than 1,000 self-propelled artillery systems, 635 towed guns and 237 multiple rocket launchers. The figures represent estimated inventories and not necessarily the number of systems available for operational use at any given time.
Turkey's equipment is a mix of older Western systems and newer generations of domestically produced platforms. For decades, Ankara relied heavily on American and European weapons, but in recent years it has invested enormous sums in an effort to reduce that dependence, from tanks and armored vehicles to missiles, air defense systems, military electronics and unmanned systems.
The result is a military that seeks not only to be large but also to be capable of maintaining and upgrading a growing share of its systems on its own.
More than 1,100 aircraft and the F-35 dream
According to Global Firepower estimates, the Turkish military has about 1,101 aircraft. The figure includes 201 fighter aircraft, 84 transport planes, 301 training aircraft and 509 helicopters, including 111 attack helicopters. Here, too, the figure represents the total inventory and not necessarily actual operational readiness. The site estimates, for example, that about 141 of the 201 fighter aircraft would be available under its assumed readiness scenario.
The backbone of Turkey's fighter fleet remains its F-16s, but Ankara is pursuing two tracks simultaneously: an effort to rejoin the American F-35 fighter jet program, from which it was removed following its purchase of the Russian S-400 system, and the development of its own indigenous fighter jet, the KAAN. The KAAN made its first flight in 2024 and is one of the Turkish defense industry's flagship projects. Ankara sees it as a key component of its plan to reduce dependence on foreign fighter aircraft, although the domestic project still relies on American components, most notably General Electric engines.
At the same time, Turkey continues to press Washington to return to the F-35 program. U.S. President Donald Trump expressed openness at the NATO summit in Ankara to allowing the sale of the aircraft to Turkey, but the path remains fraught with legal and political obstacles, including over the S-400 issue. Israel strongly opposes the move out of concern that it could undermine its qualitative military edge in the region, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly voiced his opposition.
The force that changed the battlefield: Drones
If there is one field in which Turkey has quickly become a global name, it is unmanned aerial vehicles. Turkish company Baykar, the manufacturer of the Bayraktar family, turned the TB2 into one of the world's best-known drones following its use in a series of conflicts and later developed more advanced systems, including the TB3.
Turkish drones have become not only an operational tool but also an export engine and a diplomatic asset. Turkey markets its systems to dozens of countries and has emerged in this field as a significant competitor to Israeli defense industries in the global market. According to Reuters, Turkish defense industry exports reached about $10 billion in 2025, triple the 2021 figure, and Ankara is now seeking further expansion in European and global markets.
17 frigates, 14 submarines and a ship turned drone carrier
The sea is also a central component of Turkey's power projection strategy. According to Global Firepower, the navy has 192 vessels, including 17 frigates, nine corvettes and 14 submarines. Turkey operates its naval forces across three main theaters — the Black Sea, Aegean Sea and Mediterranean — and its location allows it to control the only maritime passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
One of the navy's most prominent platforms is the TCG Anadolu, a multipurpose amphibious assault ship and the largest vessel in the Turkish fleet. After Turkey was removed from the F-35 program, it developed, among other things, a concept under which the ship could serve as a naval base for operating unmanned aircraft.
During the EFES-2026 exercise held in May, a Bayraktar TB3 was operated from the ship as part of a combat scenario. Earlier, during a NATO exercise in the Baltic Sea, a TB3 took off autonomously from Anadolu's short deck and struck maritime targets. Through this, Turkey is seeking to develop a relatively new model of naval power: a large ship that extends its operational reach through an array of armed drones.
4,500 companies and more than 1,400 projects
One of the deepest changes in Turkey's balance of power is not in the number of soldiers or tanks but in the factories behind them. For years, Turkey was a major customer for foreign weapons systems. Today, it is seeking to become a manufacturer and exporter in its own right.
According to data published this month by Anadolu Agency, more than 4,500 companies now operate in Turkey's defense industry, compared with just 56 in 2002, while the number of defense projects has surpassed 1,400. According to the same data, the share of locally produced components and systems has risen from about 20% two decades ago to more than 85% today.
The strategic significance is substantial: Turkey is able to produce at home an increasing share of the drones, missiles, armored vehicles, warships and electronic systems it uses while also generating revenue and political influence through their export.
And how much does it spend on defense?
Turkish defense spending has been rising sharply, although the scale varies considerably depending on the definition and source. In a NATO report on 2025 defense spending, Turkey's expenditure was estimated at about $32.6 billion at that year's prices and exchange rates, up from about $28.3 billion in 2024. NATO estimated that spending amounted to about 2.33% of GDP. The figures for 2024 and 2025 were identified in the report as estimates.
Other estimates put Turkey's defense budget higher. Global Firepower, for example, estimates 2026 spending at about $51.4 billion. The discrepancy is due in part to differences in definitions, budget years and calculation methods, meaning comparisons between sources should be made cautiously.
Mass, geography, experience and industry
So what makes the Turkish military particularly powerful? First and foremost, mass. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, hundreds of thousands of reservists, thousands of armored vehicles and the ability to mobilize manpower on a scale that few countries in the region can approach. The second advantage is geography: Turkey sits at the intersection of Europe, Asia and the Middle East and controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. It borders, among others, Syria, Iraq, Iran, Georgia and Bulgaria and lies within close reach of the Caucasus, Balkans and eastern Mediterranean.
The third advantage is operational experience. The Turkish military has spent years fighting the Kurdistan Workers' Party, carried out a series of operations beyond the country's borders, maintains forces and conducts operations in northern Syria and Iraq and has been involved, directly or indirectly, in additional theaters. The fourth is the defense industry. Unlike a large military that is entirely dependent on external supplies, Turkey is now able to produce an increasing share of its own weapons systems. That does not eliminate its dependence on foreign technology in certain areas, but it gives Ankara significantly greater freedom of action than it had in the past.
The fifth advantage is NATO. Turkey has been a member of the alliance since 1952, hosts NATO Allied Land Command in Izmir and is a key component of the alliance's southern flank. Membership provides it with joint training, common military standards, intelligence sharing and cooperation with some of the world's most advanced militaries.
Still, numbers alone can be misleading. The Turkish military has equipment from different generations, some of it old, and not every tank, aircraft or vessel listed in its inventory is fully operational. In modern warfare, the question is not simply how many platforms exist, but how many are available, how well protected they are, what intelligence is available to them and how effectively they can operate together on a single network with the air force, navy, drones, artillery and air defense systems.
But even with that caveat, the picture is clear: Turkey in 2026 is much more than a "large military." It is a regional military power with enormous manpower, thousands of combat platforms, significant air and naval forces, global leadership in drones and a rapidly growing defense industry. As relations with Israel grow more strained and Turkish influence in Syria expands, that power is becoming for Jerusalem less of a theoretical statistic and more of a strategic consideration that is increasingly difficult to ignore.

"Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," Zelensky said.
"For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264," he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of 300 for the upcoming winter.
The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles amid its war on Iran and has been resistant to release large numbers to Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.
Civilian deaths in the four-and-a-half-year-long war have surged to their highest since the first months of the invasion amid the uptick in Russian strikes, according to verified statistics from the United Nations.
Ukraine will on Monday host a meeting of its European allies to discuss how to pressure Russia to end its invasion.

articles.title: Greece moves Patriot battery to Crete as Iran threatens US bases in Europe
articles.body:
After the Iranian threat, Bulgaria announced that two U.S. refueling aircraft had been evacuated from the country — but Greece is instead bolstering its defenses: According to reports in Greece, the country has moved a Patriot air defense battery from the island of Karpathos to Crete to strengthen defenses around the Souda Bay area in northwestern Crete, which is considered strategically important. The battery, including personnel and equipment, was moved overnight and is expected to be deployed near the military base at Souda.
According to Greek reports, the decision was made following threats by senior Iranian officials against U.S. bases in Europe, while Greek military forces remain on heightened alert. Assessments indicate that Iran still has a significant number of ballistic missiles with ranges exceeding 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles), putting targets in southeastern Europe within their reach.
The Patriot battery was deployed to Karpathos in March as part of Greece’s efforts to strengthen its defenses against ballistic missile threats. According to the report, Athens is in contact with the United States and Israel regarding potential threats to facilities in Greece and Cyprus and is also considering helping Bulgaria’s air defense system if an official request is received. The close ties between Greece and Israel, including in the face of threats from Turkey, have been reported on numerous occasions in the past.
Bulgaria, meanwhile, announced Saturday that two U.S. military refueling aircraft whose deployment at Bezmer Air Base in southeastern Bulgaria last month had angered Iran were evacuated and moved to another location. The announcement by Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov came several days after the British Financial Times reported that Iran was considering targeting U.S. assets in southeastern Europe, including Bulgaria and Cyprus, in the event of renewed escalation with the United States.
Bulgaria approved the deployment of two KC-135 military aircraft a month ago. The aircraft are among those used to refuel fighter jets, including on their way to carry out strikes in Iran. Sofia has consistently insisted that the aircraft deployed on its territory were used only for training missions in the airspace of allied countries and not for strikes against Iran, which are not currently taking place amid the tense pause in fighting with the United States. Iran, however, reacted sharply, claiming that the presence of U.S. military aircraft in the country made Bulgaria a partner in “aggression and war crimes.”
Meanwhile, following U.S. President Donald Trump’s declaration of an “economic D-Day” against Iran, Tehran has continued its verbal attacks while the situation on the ground remains relatively quiet. Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said the U.S. president’s remarks “about economic warfare are a tacit admission of the humiliating defeat in the military arena. If you had won on the military front, you would not have needed to launch an economic war. We have a scenario for every hostile action by the enemy. There is no concern on the economic front.”
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf took a jab at the U.S. announcements that talks had been frozen in a post on X: “What’s the plan for bonds, import frozen yields? Frozen homebuyers for housing? Frozen paychecks for wages? A frozen foreign policy delivers a frozen economy. The only thing still moving? The Iran boomerang.”
But while the Twitter battles continue, Iran’s economic crisis is becoming increasingly apparent. The U.S. dollar reached an exchange rate of 2 million rials on Iran’s free market, crossing a threshold it had approached in recent days. According to Iran International, the dollar traded at around 1.865 million rials at the beginning of last week, meaning it rose by more than 7% in less than a week. In just one year, it has more than doubled in value, after trading at 958,000 rials during the same period last year.
Just last week, President Masoud Pezeshkian, a relatively moderate figure within the regime but one considered to have limited influence, again called for an end to the war. In remarks quoted by Iranian media, Pezeshkian said his government was “trying to solve the problems” currently facing Iran’s economy. He added: “During this period, despite all the problems, we have had many achievements that have not been addressed. We do not deny the shortcomings and deficiencies, but we are trying to move the country forward.”

articles.title: Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
articles.body:
A helicopter prepares to drop water on a fire at Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries' complex near Podolsk, outside Moscow, on Aug. 16, 2026. | Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP via Getty Images
For most of Russia’s years-long war against Ukraine, Russian civilians have been relatively insulated from Kyiv’s attacks. That is changing.
Since July, Kyiv has broadened its long-range drone campaign beyond conventional military targets, intensifying strikes on Russia’s oil and gas industry and hitting the vast warehouses of Wildberries, Russia’s answer to Amazon.
While these are primarily intended to cause economic damage, in the words of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, “to bring the war back home – to Russia,” they also mark another important shift. Ukrainian authorities are increasingly seeing Russian civilian casualties as a price they are prepared to pay for taking the war deeper into enemy territory.
Advertisement
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.
Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.
Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.
Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images
There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.
“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”
Advertisement
“But we know that Russia has been systematically targeting Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure and civilian districts with the deliberate intent to cause civilian casualties,” she added. “That’s an important underlying distinction to draw.”
On Friday, a Russian drone attack on a busy shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, left 16 people dead and more than a 130 wounded, including children. The strike was a double-tap — that’s when second attack on a target is conducted around half-an-hour later and is designed to catch first responders, a tactic used frequently in northern Syria.
The damage done to a shopping mall following a Russian strike in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine is pictured on Aug. 22, 2026. | Yan Dobronosov/AFP via Getty Images
Since the war began, Russian officials have consistently denied their forces intentionally target civilians and Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has instead accused Ukraine of deploying troops and heavy weapons close to civilian infrastructure.
Russia has “a clear pattern” of targeting Kyiv and other urban centers with large civilian populations, Rosemary DiCarlo, the U.N. under-secretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the U.N. Security Council in July.
The U.N. has verified that at least 16,874 Ukrainian civilians, including 820 children, have been killed since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale assault on the country in 2022. Ukrainians believe the toll is likely higher, arguing there are many unrecorded deaths near the front lines and on territory occupied by Russian forces.
Advertisement
DiCarlo also expressed concerns about Ukraine’s drone attacks. “Any attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a clear violation of international humanitarian law,” she said.
It is an argument that infuriates Ukrainian officials, who bristle when asked about the risks to Russian civilians with the tactical switch. Even asking the question triggers accusations of echoing Moscow propagandists. “You are helping Russia by pushing this civilian stuff,” a presidential aide said. He declined to answer when asked whether Ukrainian commanders adhere to any pre-strike procedures to assess risks to civilians.
The change in tactics has alarmed some European officials, according to Adrian Karatnycky, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and author of Battleground Ukraine, who regularly meets with senior European officials and diplomats. “They have always been low-risk and fearful of Russian escalation,” he said.
The shift, he added, has been enabled by Ukraine’s growing ability to manufacture its own long-range drones and by cuts in U.S. assistance that have reduced Washington’s leverage over Kyiv. “There will be noncombatant casualties, but in an existential war you can’t fight with a hand tied behind your back,” Karatnycky said. “Ukraine’s ability to counterpunch is a relatively new phenomenon.”
How will the Ukrainian attacks play out in Russia — will they weaken Putin politically? Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former U.K. diplomat now at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, said Kyiv must try to minimize civilian casualties with the long-range drone campaign.
“There are some risks,” he said. “As we know from the history of warfare, the bombing of civilians tends to actually harden people’s resistance rather than weaken it. Just think of the London Blitz, but also Ukraine now. And second, there is a danger of losing what still is a remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine.”
“But you cannot wage war without casualties,” he added.

articles.title: Ukraine targets Russia’s Amazon rivals as drone war hits home front
articles.body:
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday as another drone attack struck warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon, the latest target in Kyiv’s campaign to undermine the Russian economy and the sense of security that Vladimir Putin’s citizens had largely enjoyed until now.
Images and videos from Russia showed one warehouse in the Makhachkala area of Dagestan on fire Monday. The company said it had temporarily closed additional warehouses in nearby parts of the Caucasus, although it said those facilities had not been damaged.
Ukraine has in recent months been waging what it calls a campaign to “bring the war to the Russian rear,” seeking to exact a price from ordinary Russians by sending explosive drones at targets deep inside the country, striking oil facilities and causing a fuel crisis, and setting fire to merchandise warehouses that serve as an important artery of the Russian economy.
After weeks in which Ukraine systematically attacked at least 24 huge warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, sometimes dubbed the “Russian Amazon,” destroying goods and facilities and causing billions of dollars in damage, the Ukrainian military has in recent days begun targeting warehouses belonging to Ozon, another Russian e-commerce giant and the country’s second-largest after Wildberries.
Ozon also operates pickup points and parcel lockers throughout Russia. Kyiv has justified attacks on both companies by saying they are also used to transfer military equipment to Russian troops at the front.
Ukraine’s military officially announced its new campaign against Ozon on Saturday. In a statement, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said: “After Ukrainian units struck 15 of Wildberries’ largest logistics centers, now it is Ozon’s turn.”
Ukraine struck an Ozon logistics center in the Samara region that same day. A drone was later reported to have exploded and sparked a fire at an Ozon logistics center in the neighboring Orenburg region. On Sunday, another drone caused a major blaze at an Ozon facility in the Krasnodar region. A logistics center near an Ozon facility outside St. Petersburg was also hit. Ozon says six of its facilities have been damaged so far.
Russian President Vladimir Putin addressed the attacks on merchandise warehouses last Wednesday, when they were still focused exclusively on Wildberries, promising that the government would help rebuild the logistics centers damaged in the strikes. He acknowledged that damage had been caused but sought to play down its scale, saying it would not have critical consequences.
On Saturday, Putin warned that by attacking Wildberries and Ozon warehouses as well as oil facilities deep inside Russia, Ukraine had “opened Pandora’s box.” He said Moscow would respond by “striking the most sensitive sectors of Ukraine’s economy.”
Following Monday morning’s attacks on Ozon facilities, shares in the e-commerce giant fell 12% on the Moscow Exchange. Shares in its main controlling shareholder, private investment company AFK Sistema, fell nearly 13%.
Ukraine marks Independence Day with 6.1 million euros from Europe
The growing number of Ukrainian drone launches against civilian targets in Russia is also taking an increasing toll in human life.
Russia said Monday morning that two children were killed in an overnight Ukrainian drone attack in which Kyiv launched more than 350 drones deep into Russian territory.
According to Moscow, drone debris fell on a children’s day care center in Krasnodar, killing two children and injuring seven others and two adults.
Ukraine said it also struck two Russian MiG-29 fighter jets and two Russian vessels in the Black Sea with drones Monday.
Russian attacks on Ukraine, meanwhile, have continued unabated. Three people were reported killed Sunday night by Russian fire on the outskirts of Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine.
Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union until 1991, with Russia its dominant republic, and the two countries maintained close and friendly relations until 2014.
After Ukraine’s pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych was ousted in a popular uprising early that year, Russia seized Crimea, which until then had been part of Ukraine, and annexed it, arguing that the peninsula rightfully belonged to Russia and had been improperly transferred to Kyiv during the Soviet era.
Russia also sent forces into the Luhansk and Donetsk regions of eastern Ukraine, home to large Russian-speaking populations, saying it was acting to protect them from the new government.
After years of fighting in eastern Ukraine, and amid discussions over Kyiv moving closer to the West and potentially joining NATO, which Moscow views as its greatest security threat, Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Contrary to his expectations and those of others, Russian forces failed to capture the capital, Kyiv. Although Russia seized parts of four Ukrainian regions and forcibly annexed them, the Ukrainian military proved resilient and prevented the country from falling under Russian control.
As the months passed, Ukraine began carrying out an increasing number of retaliatory operations deep inside Russia, including targeted killings of senior figures and ground incursions. But Kyiv has inflicted most of its damage on Putin’s government through drone attacks, which have intensified in recent months.
Estimates indicate that hundreds of thousands of soldiers on each side have been killed since the war began, along with large numbers of civilians.
Monday’s attacks came as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day. Leaders from several European countries and institutions that support Kyiv in its war against Russia arrived in the Ukrainian capital for the occasion, including new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the leaders of Luxembourg, Moldova and Estonia and European Council President António Costa.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced Monday that the commission had approved a 6.1 million-euro aid package for Ukraine’s defense.
“On Ukraine’s Independence Day, we show our unfaltering support. Today, we approved €6.1 billion for the air and missile defence systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs,” von der Leyen said. “Europe stands with you today, tomorrow, and for as long as it takes.”

articles.title: Russia claims it shot down Flamingo missile with gunfire
articles.body:
- Russian officials claim a volunteer air defense unit in Kursk Region shot down a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile with machine-gun fire overnight August 22 to 23, 2026.
- The claim, unverified by independent sources, has not been confirmed by Ukraine, and the missile's reported speed was below the Flamingo's stated cruise speed.
Russian officials say a volunteer air defense unit in Kursk Region shot down a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile using machine-gun fire during an overnight attack this weekend, an unusual claim for a weapon Russia has typically engaged with surface-to-air missile systems.
Kursk Region Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein said the intercept happened overnight Saturday into Sunday, August 22 to 23, 2026. According to Khinshtein, a mobile air defense team from the BARS-Kursk brigade, a unit made up largely of local residents from the border region, received an alert about an incoming strike and detected a “huge” missile flying at roughly 500 km/h (310 mph) at an altitude below 50 m (164 feet). The team engaged the missile with gunfire, causing it to lose altitude and crash into a wooded area, Khinshtein said.
As evidence, Russian sources published footage recorded on a thermal camera, showing the missile passing overhead and then falling. Separate footage showed what was described as wreckage from the missile itself.
The exact date of the strike has not been independently confirmed, and no outside party has verified that small-arms fire, rather than a surface-to-air missile system or an aircraft, brought the missile down. Some pieces of the recovered wreckage reportedly showed damage patterns consistent with hits from a large-caliber machine gun, though this detail also comes from the Russian side and has not been independently examined. At least one Russian commentator described the released footage as “ambiguous.”
The Flamingo, built by Ukrainian defense firm Fire Point and first unveiled in August 2025, is a large ground-launched cruise missile. It weighs about 6,000 kg (13,200 pounds) at launch, carries a warhead of roughly 1,150 kg (2,540 pounds), and has a stated range of 3,000 km (1,860 miles). Its listed cruise speed is 850 to 900 km/h (530 to 560 mph), well above the roughly 500 km/h Khinshtein described for the intercepted missile, and its flight ceiling reaches 5,000 m (16,400 feet). Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called it the country’s “most successful missile.”
Russia has claimed multiple Flamingo intercepts since the missile entered use, generally citing dedicated air defense systems. In October 2025, Russian media said a Buk surface-to-air missile system downed a Flamingo at an altitude of about 100 m (330 feet). In February 2026, Russian officials reported additional intercepts during a large-scale missile alert spanning 13 regions.

articles.title: Ukraine backers gather in Kiev as war escalates, air defence runs low
articles.body:
Ukraine hosts a meeting of its key European backers on Monday to press for critical air-defence supplies and more pressure on Moscow, with Russian attacks killing more civilians than at any time since the first months of the invasion.
The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be in Kiev for his first international trip since taking office, and several other leaders are expected to join remotely.
EU Council President Antonio Costa is also due in Kiev for the talks, which come amid the latest, deadly escalation of the war.
Russia has been pounding Kiev with ballistic missiles in recent weeks, and reportedly killing dozens of citizens in the capital.
Civilian deaths have risen to their highest levels since the first months of the Russia–Ukraine war in 2022, amid intensified Russian strikes.
After almost every attack - which sees tens of thousands hunker in the Kiev metro system and many more in basements and other shelters across the city – Zelenskyy has issued public pleas for more air-defence support.
Ahead of the meeting, Ukraine has forged ahead with its campaign against Russia's logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early Monday at its warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.
Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack killed two children and wounded nine others.
UK, French support
Ukraine celebrates independence day on Monday, which also marks exactly four-and-a-half years since Russia began its military campaign on February 24, 2022.
"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve," Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kiev.
"We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
Diplomacy on ending the conflict - Europe's largest since World War II - is effectively frozen.
Russia is demanding territorial and political concessions that Kiev has rejected, claiming as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack.
Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorising defence firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile.
And on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
"It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression," Macron wrote on X.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in the dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop.
Kiev's homegrown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems - chiefly, US Patriot interceptors - to protect its skies.
But due to shortfalls globally since the US launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed.
Ukraine's missiles shortfall
Ahead of the meeting, Zelenskyy revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
"Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 - 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," Zelenskyy said.
"For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264," he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.
The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles during its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites - including oil refineries and retail warehouses.
The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.
Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshalling support to Ukraine as uncertainty persists over US commitments under Donald Trump.

articles.title: Here are some of Trump’s options as he prepares to increase economic pressure on Iran
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has vowed to hit Iran hard economically, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Washington would impose measures on Tehran that have "never been seen" as soon as next week.
Bessent is due to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday.
The United States, United Nations and European Union have applied sanctions, implemented trade embargoes and frozen assets since the late 1970s over Iran's nuclear program, human rights violations and support for militant groups.
Since the Iran war began in February, Washington has levied additional maritime, energy, and financial sanctions and started a naval blockade.
Data from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) shows the agency has imposed sanctions on more than 1,000 people, vessels, and aircraft since Trump began his second term.
Recent measures have targeted Iran's shadow oil fleet; shipping insurers; entities and people enabling Iran's acquisition of weapons; and digital exchanges, freezing an estimated $500 billion in Iran-linked cryptocurrency.
Iran has denounced US plans to announce new sanctions that could put further strain on the Islamic Republic's economy.
Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorized oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway, and Iran's economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions.
Experts say the Trump administration also can try these options:
Sanctions on Chinese 'Teapot' refineries
Chinese independent refineries known as "teapots" account for a quarter of Chinese refinery capacity. They operate with narrow and sometimes negative profit margins.
China buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Independent refiners absorb much of this trade, exposing them to so-called secondary measures that penalize entities helping a primary sanctions target.
Past US sanctions have deterred larger independent refiners from buying Iranian oil. But the independent refineries are somewhat immune since they have little exposure to the US financial system, sanctions experts say.
OFAC has imposed secondary sanctions on smaller China- and Hong Kong-based entities accused of processing billions of dollars in Iranian oil and helping to fund weapons procurement.
The Treasury Department has warned two larger Chinese banks they could face secondary sanctions if Iranian funds were found moving through their systems, but has stopped short of designating them.
Hitting those two banks, which US officials have not publicly identified, or imposing other sanctions could have a chilling effect on bigger financial institutions, sanctions experts said, although they warned it could also trigger retaliatory actions by Beijing.
Trump administration officials have sought to play down tensions between Washington and Beijing ahead of an expected meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping later this year. They worry that China could curtail exports of critical minerals that are essential to advanced technology production at a time when the US and Western allies are still trying to develop their own supplies.
US would target Iranian, Chinese, Gulf, entities and individuals helping Iran evade sanctions
The United States could continue targeting Iranian individuals and entities, as well as others in China and the Gulf, that are helping Tehran evade sanctions to collect revenues for its war effort.
The Treasury Department recently issued sanctions against firms that are springing up to facilitate Iran's trading of oil revenue for imports. But such measures amount to a "whack-a-mole" approach that has not altered Iran's behavior, said Brett Erickson, managing principal of Obsidian Risk Advisors, noting that Tehran simply creates new entities to replace them.
Miad Maleki, a sanctions expert with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Bessent was likely signaling a sharpened enforcement push against oil shippers, purchasers and currency exchangers who help Iran pay for its imports.
Further aviation sanctions were also possible, aimed at degrading Iran's ability to move trade now that the US has blockaded shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, he added.
Floating the idea of a land blockade
Some US and Israeli officials have floated the prospect of a land blockade, which would require assistance from Iran's neighbors: Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, and Armenia.
The Trump administration has varying degrees of closeness with all those countries except Afghanistan, but that border is mountainous and extremely difficult to patrol anyway.
Trump may have leverage over Pakistan, which recently sought a $10 billion currency swap line from Treasury, and Turkey, which is seeking to rejoin the US F-35 warplane program.
A land blockade could increase pressure on the Iranian people by halting their imports of food, energy and textiles, but experts say such a move would be difficult to execute and might not result in protests or internal pressure.
Imposing tariffs on goods from countries that do business with Iran
Trump has repeatedly threatened tariffs on goods from countries that do business with Iran, although the Supreme Court struck down the legal basis for such taxes.
The Senate passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill last week that included new Iran sanctions and would give Trump new tariff powers that he could potentially use against countries that aid Iran's commerce and weapons procurement.
That legislation must still pass the US House of Representatives, which could prove challenging given widespread concerns among Democrats and some Republicans about the tariff measures.

articles.title: Andy Burnham arrives in Ukraine with plans to share UK blueprints for long-range missiles - Europe live
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Europe. I am kicking us off but Jakub Krupa will be taking over a little later on.
UK prime minister Andy Burnham arrived in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Monday alongside a number of European leaders to mark the country’s independence day.
Burnham was photographed at Kyiv railway station shaking hands with Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, who said Burnham was to be joined by António Costa, president of the European Council; Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg; Maia Sandu, the president of Moldova; and Alar Karis, the president of Estonia.
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds. In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side,” Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X announcing their arrival.
“And today, we know for sure who our true friends are.”

articles.title: Cheap 'Guardian' interceptors developed by Florida start-up could turn tables on Iranian drones
articles.body:
Inexpensive interceptors developed by a small start-up based in West Palm Beach, Florida, could be used to counter the threat posed by Iranian drones, according to a report by The New York Times on Sunday.
Powerus has been building its drone interceptors at a United Arab Emirates facility since July, where it produces 3-D printed components and assembles them into the finished product. The design, known as the "Guardian," sells for around $5,000.
The report cited a Powerus spokesperson, who said the company produces 3,000 interceptors a month and hopes to increase that to 15,000 a month by 2027. This is helped by the product's modular design, as the readily available components easily snap together.
According to the NYT, Powerus based the Guardian on a Ukrainian drone interceptor which showed promise against Russian suicide drones. The company's website describes the interceptor as having a top "burst" speed of 340 kph, a 160 kph cruise speed, a range of 15 kilometers, 28 minutes of operational endurance, and "hundreds" of confirmed interceptions.
The NYT noted that the Guardians, originally produced in the United States, are not a complete solution to the interceptor shortage currently facing the US military after its war with Iran. The design cannot counter ballistic missiles and other larger threats, which are better suited to more expensive options, such as Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3.
US company builds cheap interceptors as Pentagon hits shortage
That said, the design still holds promise, with Powerus signing a $22.3 million contract on Thursday to protect Middle Eastern oil and gas infrastructure.
“This commercial contract reflects the direction we believe the counter-drone market is heading: toward integrated, networked protection of critical oil and gas infrastructure,” said company co-founder and COO Brett Velicovich.
“We are starting with the capabilities our customer needs today while providing an architecture that can expand as the threat and operational requirements evolve," he added.
"Powerus is bringing US-based engineering, manufacturing and technology to help protect the operations that power that infrastructure."
Price competition for interceptor, UAE-interested in further involvement
Another spokesperson told the NYT that the company faces price competition, with a California-based drone interceptor developer listing a basic model for about $5,000.
According to the report, the UAE has recently sought out opportunities for the development and assembly of interceptors on its own territory, having faced thousands of drones and ballistic missiles fired by Iran recently.
UAE seeking 'sovereign capability,' regional researcher says
International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) research associate Albert Vidal, based in the region, told the NYT that the primary goal of constructing the interceptors in the UAE is to establish "sovereign capability."
“The reaction in the UAE is: ‘We’re going to continue buying as much as we can from the US, but we will also buy from other players, and we are also going to produce stuff at home,’” he said.

articles.title: On Independence Day, EU adds $7B for Ukraine
articles.body:
- The European Commission approved $7 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine on August 24, 2026, covering air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.
- The funding is part of a $105 billion Ukraine Support Loan, and adds to $18.68 billion in previously approved procurement, of which $9.75 billion has been disbursed.
The European Commission approved €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in new defense procurement funding for Ukraine on August 24, 2026, the same day Ukraine marked its Independence Day.
The money covers air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen tied the timing directly to the war.
“On Ukraine’s Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete. Today, we have approved €6.1 billion for the air and missile defence systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs. As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it.”
The Commission cited 376 missile strikes recorded against Ukraine in July alone as the backdrop for the approval. Most of the procurement will go to companies within the EU defense industrial base.
The €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) comes out of the Ukraine Support Loan, a €90 billion ($105.08 billion) package the European Parliament and Council established under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 in February 2026. The loan splits into two tracks: one for Ukraine’s defense capabilities and defense industrial capacity, the other for keeping the Ukrainian state functioning, covering public services and broader economic resilience. Under the loan, €30 billion ($35.03 billion) is earmarked for budgetary aid and €60 billion ($70.05 billion) for defense spending across 2026 and 2027, with €28.3 billion ($33.04 billion) of that defense allocation set for this year.
Ukraine submitted its financing strategy for the loan in March 2026. The Council followed with an implementing decision on April 23, 2026, allocating up to €45 billion ($52.54 billion) for the year. That figure breaks down into €16.7 billion ($19.50 billion) in budget support, split evenly between the Ukraine Facility and Macro Financial Assistance at roughly €8.35 billion ($9.75 billion) each, and €28.3 billion ($33.04 billion) for defense industrial capacity.
Today’s €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) adds to €16 billion ($18.68 billion) in procurement plans the Commission had already approved before this announcement. Of that earlier total, €8.35 billion ($9.75 billion) has already been disbursed to Ukraine.
To draw down the new funds, Ukraine has to submit signed contracts with defense companies to the Commission. Commission staff review each contract before releasing money, a step meant to confirm the funds go toward the procurements Ukraine agreed on with member states and the Commission.
The Commission has flagged Russia’s growing use of ballistic missiles and jet-engined drones as a reason EU suppliers need to move faster. It is pressing companies to draw down existing stockpiles, reorder production priorities, and expand output to keep pace with Ukraine’s needs.
The defense funding track under the loan is also meant to do more than supply weapons for the current fight. The Commission describes it as reconstructing and modernizing Ukraine’s defense technology and industrial base, with an eye toward folding that base into the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base over time.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €220.2 billion ($257.19 billion) in total support to Ukraine. That figure includes €3.8 billion ($4.44 billion) drawn from the proceeds of immobilized Russian state assets.

articles.title: Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
articles.body:
Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
Syria’s foreign minister meets with an Israeli delegation led by the chief of the Mossad to de-escalate tensions after an Israeli strike near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has met with Israeli intelligence officials in Jordan, according to Syrian state media, as the two sides work to de-escalate tensions following an Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Sana news agency, citing a diplomatic source, said the talks were mediated by the United States and involved a “high-level Israeli delegation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israel bombs Syria as US envoy says base attack aimed at ‘baiting’ Turkiye
- list 2 of 3Envoy says Israel did not give the US notice before strikes on Syrian base
- list 3 of 3Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
The AFP news agency reported that al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman.
According to Sana, the discussions “focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations” as well as “reviving negotiations for a lasting security agreement between the two sides”.
They also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Turkiye and to prevent their rivalry from spilling onto Syrian territory, Sana reported.
The US has sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa for more than a year. Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and sent troops into a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
It also bombed the Abu Duhur airbase in northwestern Idlib on Thursday, claiming the attack was to prevent Turkish troops from deploying at the base, a claim Syria and Turkiye have denied.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders.
According to Sana, the Syrian side stressed during Sunday’s talks “that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests”. The Syrian side rejected “any arrangements or mechanisms that would restrict these sovereign rights,” it said.
Syria’s immediate priorities in the talks remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before al-Assad’s overthrow and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement, Sana reported.
The Syrian officials also reaffirmed Damascus’s sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, it added.
Israel’s ‘red lines’
Israeli media reported that the talks were “positive” and said Israeli officials had adopted a number of red lines going into talks.
These include preventing Turkish military activity in Syria, keeping the Syrian side of the Golan Heights demilitarised, “ensuring the security” of Syria’s Druze community and preventing the Syrian army from acquiring certain strategic weapons systems.
They also conditioned any withdrawal from Syrian territories occupied by Israel on “diplomatic achievements”.
During previous rounds of US-mediated talks, Syria and Israel had agreed on a joint mechanism to share intelligence and defuse tensions. But the negotiations froze at the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, without a date set for resumption.
In an interview published ahead of the meeting, al-Shaibani told Reuters news agency that Damascus did not trust Israel, but that the door remained open for diplomacy. He said Syria had cut off contact entirely after the Israeli attack on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Al-Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only UN forces would be present.
Hassan Mneimneh, a political analyst and researcher at the Middle East Institute, told Al Jazeera that the current round of talks was unlikely to de-escalate tensions given Israel’s track record.
“It’s quite the opposite, meaning now that Syria has indicated its desire to have the situation de-escalate, Israel is likely to bring in more demands and have the Americans basically negotiate these new demands with Syria, against any kind of expansion of Turkish presence in the north and beyond the north,” he said.
Mneimneh added that Syria was “afraid that the country will become a battlefield” between Israel and Turkiye and was concerned about Israel’s territorial grab in the country, stretching “all the way to Hermon, to Jabal al-Sheikh in its totality almost, and all the way to three southern provinces”.
So, from the Syrian perspective, Mneimneh added, the talks with Israel seem to be aimed at avoiding “the disintegration of Syrian authority” as well as ensuring any conflict between Israel and Turkiye does not prevent Syria from “forming, establishing, consolidating polity after the fall of” al-Assad.

articles.title: U.S. Unveils AIM-424 Malice: Ultra-Long-Range Missile With Range of Over 463 km
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy’s Naval Aviation branch has unveiled a new ultra-long-range air-to-air missile, the AIM-424 Malice, with a stated range of more than 463 km.
The relevant photographs were published by DVIDS, the official media platform of the U.S. Department of Defense.
The missile was shown on two types of carrier-based fighter aircraft: the F-35C Lightning II and the F/A-18E Super Hornet.
The missile was developed and manufactured by the U.S. company Raytheon. It is powered by a solid-propellant rocket motor.
The missile is 4.11 meters long, has a diameter of 0.34 meters, and a wingspan of 0.67 meters. Its launch mass is 680.4 kg. The missile has a stated range of more than 463 km and is equipped with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
Although photographs of the AIM-424 Malice were not released until August 22, 2026, available information indicates that testing of the missile began as early as the winter of 2026.
There is currently no detailed information regarding the completion of the missile’s integration with its carrier aircraft. However, the released photographs demonstrate that the F/A-18E Super Hornet can accommodate at least four AIM-424 Malice missiles.
The carrier-based F-35C can carry these missiles in its internal weapons bays, allowing the aircraft to maintain a low observable signature while conducting combat missions.
It is currently unknown what specific role the AIM-424 Malice will play in the U.S. Navy’s weapons inventory. The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy have traditionally developed their own air-launched missiles in parallel. Naval aviation already employs the AIM-120, while the U.S. Navy recently unveiled and test-fired the long-range AIM-174 during an exercise.
The AIM-424 Malice could potentially complement the AIM-174 or partially replace it.
In terms of design, the new missile more closely resembles conventional air-to-air missiles, whereas the AIM-174 was developed from the ship-launched SM-6 surface-to-air missile. The latter is also capable of intercepting ballistic targets, making it an important component in countering Chinese anti-ship ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the U.S. Air Force is developing its own long-range AIM-260 missile. It is likewise intended to engage targets at extended ranges. However, no official data on its range or other key performance characteristics have been released to date.

articles.title: Minister tells social media firms to take down dangerous driving content in wake of fatal A66 crash in Middlesborough – UK politics live
articles.body:
Social media firms told to take down dangerous driving content in wake of fatal A66 crash
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The government has told social media companies to take down content showing people driving the wrong way down roads following a fatal crash over the weekend.
Two police officers were among seven people killed when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into a force vehicle on the A66 near Middlesbrough.
There have been reports that at least one of the young men who died in the collision early on Saturday had been involved in filming dangerous driving in TikTok videos.
Asked about these reports this morning, the defence minister, Luke Pollard, said social media platforms must remove content glorifying dangerous driving or else the government will use powers under the Online Safety Act to compel them to take the videos down. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live this morning, Pollard said:
We’ve communicated to those social media platforms that have been hosting content that celebrates this type of dangerous behaviour on our roads to take down that content.
I think we all need to give the police time, but there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content. I want to see social media companies step up.
It’s one of the reasons they’ve argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves. Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads.
The issue of lax social media regulation of dangerous driving content came to prominence amid a public outcry in Ireland afterfive teenagers were killed in a head-on crash involving a car driving in the wrong direction on a motorway in County Kildare last weekend.
The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, described the head-on collision between the two cars as “horrific” and said “in some cases” vehicles were being driven on the wrong side of motorways for social media likes. TikTok declined an invitation to appear before an Irish parliamentary committee on media to discuss videos, citing the ongoing police investigation, according to Ireland’s national broadcaster, RTÉ,
Government vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairer
Lauren Almeida
The government has promised that business rate valuations will be “made fairer” for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, as Andy Burnham faces growing calls to help the UK’s struggling hospitality sector.
An independent review for England and Wales will look at improving the system for hospitality venues, which were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.
It comes after Burnham announced last month that he would cut business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April next year.
The government has faced calls to reduce the tax burden on hospitality businesses, which have also struggled to cope with rising energy and food bills in recent years.
The review, which will be led by Jerry Schurder, an independent business rates specialist, will report back to the Treasury by the end of March 2027. It will consider valuations before the next revaluation date in 2029. The rise in valuations this year will not be affected. You can read the full story here:
The prime minister will use the trip to Kyiv to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version.
While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations.
Andy Burnham will announce in Kyiv that the UK will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month.
The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years’ time.
But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.
Last week, Russia accused the UK of deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, warning that the deeper Britain’s involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.
This weekend it emerged that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador in London without naming a replacement, prompting speculation it was downgrading its diplomatic presence in the UK.
Burnham has insisted that Russian threats will not weaken British support for Ukraine, saying last week: “We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.” You can read more from my colleagues Kiran StaceyandDan Sabbagh here:
Andy Burnham arrives in Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missiles
Vivian Ho
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, arrived in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Monday alongside a number of European leaders to mark the country’s independence day.
Burnham was photographed at Kyiv railway station shaking hands with Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, who said Burnham was to be joined by António Costa, president of the European Council; Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg; Maia Sandu, the president of Moldova; and Alar Karis, the president of Estonia.
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds. In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side,” Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X announcing their arrival.
“And today, we know for sure who our true friends are.”
Burnham plans to announce during his visit that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp long-range missiles to help Ukraine build its own version – a major boost to the country’s capacity in weapons development at a crucial time in the war. You can read the latest developments in our Europe live blog:
Cleveland police and crime commissioner Matt Storey was on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme this morning to take questions on the fatal A66 crash.
Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak died when their Volkswagen Passat, believed to be using cloned plates, collided with a marked armed response vehicle early on Saturday near Middlesbrough.
Pc Matthew Blades, 37, and Pc Tom Clough, 38, who had been driving in the correct direction, were killed in the collision. They have been hailed as heroes by their families.
It has been reported that Saddington was involved in filming dangerous driving in TikTok videos before the fatal crash took place – although this has not been confirmed by police. Storey acknowledged the reports about the TikTok videos, but urged people to avoid speculation. He said:
Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it’s absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they’re behind the wheel of a vehicle.
And for somebody to be filming themselves or doing anything like that is absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that. And it is a worrying situation if that’s becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous.
Social media firms told to take down dangerous driving content in wake of fatal A66 crash
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The government has told social media companies to take down content showing people driving the wrong way down roads following a fatal crash over the weekend.
Two police officers were among seven people killed when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into a force vehicle on the A66 near Middlesbrough.
There have been reports that at least one of the young men who died in the collision early on Saturday had been involved in filming dangerous driving in TikTok videos.
Asked about these reports this morning, the defence minister, Luke Pollard, said social media platforms must remove content glorifying dangerous driving or else the government will use powers under the Online Safety Act to compel them to take the videos down. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live this morning, Pollard said:
We’ve communicated to those social media platforms that have been hosting content that celebrates this type of dangerous behaviour on our roads to take down that content.
I think we all need to give the police time, but there’s also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn’t celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content. I want to see social media companies step up.
It’s one of the reasons they’ve argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves. Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads.
The issue of lax social media regulation of dangerous driving content came to prominence amid a public outcry in Ireland afterfive teenagers were killed in a head-on crash involving a car driving in the wrong direction on a motorway in County Kildare last weekend.
The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, described the head-on collision between the two cars as “horrific” and said “in some cases” vehicles were being driven on the wrong side of motorways for social media likes. TikTok declined an invitation to appear before an Irish parliamentary committee on media to discuss videos, citing the ongoing police investigation, according to Ireland’s national broadcaster, RTÉ,

articles.title: The Telegraph: Russia launches wave of sabotage attacks on weapons factories in Europe
articles.body:
The Telegraph: Russia launches wave of sabotage attacks on weapons factories in Europe
Russia has launched a new wave of attacks on weapons factories in Europe, recruiting members of local criminal gangs and testing NATO's response.
Source: The Telegraph with reference to Western intelligence sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to sources, Russia has launched a series of sabotage operations at weapons factories in Europe under the cover of "plausible deniability". The Kremlin is recruiting members of local criminal gangs and carefully planning the attacks so that they do not reach the threshold that would trigger NATO's Article 5 on mutual defence.
This week, Latvia detained three of its citizens on suspicion of arson at a drone factory in neighbouring Estonia. A building belonging to Milrem Robotics – a Tallinn-based company that supplies weapons to Ukraine – was set on fire on the night of 14-15 August.
At the time of the incident, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that investigators were determining whether it was an act of sabotage and whether Russia was involved.
The arson attack targeting the Milrem Robotics building fits into a broader pattern of suspected or confirmed acts of sabotage against arms supply chains for Ukraine on the territory of NATO countries.
According to Alliance officials, these actions by the Kremlin are aimed at escalating tensions among allies and deterring support for Kyiv.
Earlier this year, a fire virtually destroyed a Czech factory that produces drones and thermal imaging equipment for Ukraine. Four suspects were detained as part of an investigation into Russian involvement.
Lithuania has also charged six individuals in connection with an attempted arson at a factory that supplies radio-wave scanners to Kyiv.
On 10 August, a powerful explosion occurred at a factory belonging to EMCO – one of the largest private weapons manufacturers in Bulgaria, which produces 155-mm artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The fire initially broke out in a lorry parked near a warehouse.
Three days later, a similar explosion occurred at an ammunition factory owned by KNDS Ammo Italy in the town of Colleferro, on the outskirts of Rome. The cause was said to be a fire that broke out in a gunpowder processing area, the origin of which remains unclear.
Italian and Bulgarian officials sought to downplay any possible Russian involvement in these incidents. However, as in the cases of Estonia, Italy and Bulgaria, Russia very rarely leaves evidence that would directly link it to the attacks.
This is because the Kremlin recruits members of local criminal gangs to carry out these sabotage operations. Officers from the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces establish contact with informants within gangs who act as intermediaries in the target country, using messaging apps such as Telegram.
It is these intermediaries who distribute local tasks among recruits, who are paid in cryptocurrency and often have no idea they are working for the Russians.
The covert nature of the attacks, organised on the Kremlin's orders, is seen as a deliberate move to sow discord among NATO allies.
Eastern member states of the Alliance, such as Poland and the Baltic countries, have been far more vocal in condemning Russian aggression in Europe. However, countries further to the west, such as Italy and Germany, are often reluctant to link these incidents to Moscow for fear of escalation. It is precisely this divide among Western allies that the Kremlin is seeking to expose.
