articles.title: Once again, Israel bombs populated Lebanese villages with prohibited white phosphorus
articles.body:
Once again, Israel bombs populated Lebanese villages with prohibited white phosphorus
TEHRAN — Israeli forces launched an extensive wave of artillery shelling and airstrikes across southern Lebanon overnight into Saturday, saturating several residential neighborhoods with banned white phosphorus munitions.
Lebanese media outlets reported severe destruction across southern border towns, including Mansouri, Majdal Zoun, and Bayt al-Sayyad. In Bayt al-Sayyad, heavy artillery strikes damaged virtually every residential property.
Israeli warplanes also carried out two air raids against the Ali al-Taher hill on the northern outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, while reconnaissance drones maintained continuous flights over the central and western sectors.
White phosphorus and systematic destruction
Israeli units fired phosphorus rounds targeting the outskirts of Dawhat Kfar Remman, the area around Dabsha hill, and the wooded zones near Ali al-Taher.
White phosphorus is an incendiary chemical compound that ignites instantly when exposed to oxygen. It produces temperatures exceeding 760 degrees Celsius, causing excruciating second- and third-degree burns deep into human bone.
Inhaling its toxic vapor inflicts severe respiratory trauma and asphyxiation. International humanitarian law strictly prohibits airburst white phosphorus over inhabited areas due to its inherently indiscriminate impact.
Rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, have repeatedly verified Israel’s deployment of white phosphorus over populated Lebanese border villages such as Kafr Kila, Mays al-Jabal, Boustane, Markaba, and Aita al-Chaab, as well as densely populated districts in Gaza.
The Israeli military has also continued waging aggressive Ground operations in south Lebanon. Infantry units advanced from Biyada toward Buyut al-Sayyid and al-Mansouri, sweeping surrounding valleys with sustained machine-gun fire.
In Zawtar al-Sharqiya, Israeli forces deliberately burned residential homes belonging to displaced Lebanese citizens, established a new military checkpoint, and systematically destroyed local farmland and olive trees.
Further artillery bombardment struck the territory situated between Beit Yahoun and Baraachit, while powerful explosions shook the towns of Kounine, Hadatha, and Aita al-Jabal.
Targeting press crews and U.S. protection
These military actions occur alongside systematic efforts to eliminate witnesses documenting the destruction.
In Beirut, media professionals and bereaved families convened at the Lebanese National Theater on Friday for a memorial titled “Martyrs of the Word and Image” to honor eleven reporters martyred by Israeli strikes.
Spokespersons for the families announced they are collecting forensic files and field testimonies to submit to the International Criminal Court, aiming to prosecute Israeli officials for premeditated attacks on press crews.
Lebanon’s UN representative Caroline Ziadeh previously documented that 28 Lebanese media workers have been killed since October 2023.
This ongoing campaign against Lebanese sovereignty operates with the full backing of the United States.
Washington continues to provide the Israeli military with heavy munitions, technical intelligence, and unconditional diplomatic cover.
By shielding Israel from UN sanctions and financing weapon shipments used against civilian infrastructure, the U.S. acts as an active partner in these documented war crimes, while it claims to facilitate diplomacy between Israel and the Lebanese government.

articles.title: A ‘Tsunami’ for Ukraine: Zelensky Rejects Wartime Elections
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky may be under pressure to hold elections in Ukraine, including from his former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov, but in remarks over the weekend, the Ukrainian President argued that doing so during the ongoing conflict with Russia would “destroy” the country.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk,” Zelensky said in remarks to journalists during a two-hour meeting Saturday—parts of which were made public on Sunday. “Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine.”
The renewed push for wartime elections was bolstered by Fedorov, who, in a video posted to social media last week, argued that "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia.” Zelensky fired Fedorov, once his longtime ally, in July over disagreements in how to run the war with Russia.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move towards elections,” Zelensky said.
Fedorov’s call for elections is the latest leadership test for Zelensky, whose five-year term expired in May 2024 but continues under wartime rules. Elections are suspended under martial law.
Zelensky recently fired a top aide amid a growing corruption scandal involving members of his office. Zelensky himself has not been implicated, but it has added to his political woes.
For the first time with journalists, Zelensky addressed the ongoing controversy involving Fedorov on Saturday, claiming that the former defense minister’s actions were misguided.
Zelensky added that “there can be no conflict at such a level between leaders,” referring to Fedorov's conflict with the former Armed Forces commander-in-chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrsky. Zelensky also replaced Syrsky last month after Fedorov’s removal spurred massive protests within the military and on the streets of Kyiv.
Syrsky was widely viewed as part of the old guard, while Fedorov had pushed for the adoption of modern warfare technology, including drones.
“I really had and still have a very positive attitude towards Mykhailo [Fedorov],” he said, according to local news outlet Interfax. “We’ve been through a lot together. But I think that he himself is going—or he's being pushed—into the wrong things.”
In a post on X, Zelensky also mentioned that the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense was under severe strain with a $27 billion shortfall.
“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the Ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half, and that money went toward drone production and other needs,” Zelensky posted. “Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented.”
Zelensky discussed the defense budget deficit during a summit with Nordic and Baltic leaders in Kyiv on Sunday, where the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden agreed to continue to provide military and financial support.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to visit Ukraine Monday, in his first international visit.
“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace,” Burnham said in a statement Monday.
Successive polls have shown a lack of public interest in holding elections during the war. The latest, conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology from July 20 to Aug. 3, shows that 57% of Ukrainians believe elections should be held after fighting has ended, down from 69% in March. Experts have previously said that the invasion, which Russian President Vladimir Putin launched in 2022, nixed the possibility of holding safe and secure elections in Ukraine.
Zelensky has denied postponing the polls to cling to power, and told reporters on Saturday that holding elections “is impossible under the conditions we have now, when Putin does not want to accept any ceasefire options.”
In the same conversation, Zelensky said he believes Russia will draft an additional 300,000 troops to fight in Ukraine after Russian parliamentary elections, which are scheduled on Sept. 18-20.
Zelensky said Russia could also draft more troops in 2027. He expects most of the additional forces to be deployed in the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, where military clashes are ongoing.

articles.title: Israel says backchannels to Turkey remain after Syria strike
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel says 'secret channels' to Turkey remain after Syria strike
An Israeli security official has said Israel has "no intention of turning Turkey into an enemy" despite striking a Syrian airbase over alleged plans by Ankara to deploy radar and air defence systems there.
The official told Israel's Kan Reshet Bet radio on Sunday that "secret channels" remained open between Israel and Turkey to exchange messages and prevent direct conflict, amid heightened tensions following the Israeli attack on Abu al-Duhur military airport in northern Syria.
However, the official warned that "when messages do not work, Israel is forced to act".
According to Kan, Israel has drawn "red lines" around any Turkish military reinforcement in Syria, particularly the deployment of air defence systems, drones or missiles that could restrict the Israeli air force's ability to operate over the country.
Israeli aircraft struck buildings and runways at Abu al-Duhur airport in eastern Idlib province last week "before the Turkish military equipment reached its destination", Kan reported.
The broadcaster said Israel had sought to send a message to Damascus that it "will not allow a new threat to be established near its borders", while stressing that Israel does not oppose the rebuilding of the Syrian army itself.
Turkey denied that it had any military presence at the airbase at the time of the attack.
"There was no Turkish military mission at the Syrian air force base before or during the Israeli attacks," Ankara said in a statement following the strike.
Kan reported on Saturday that Israeli security officials had informed the US that Turkey was preparing to install radar equipment at Abu al-Duhur, with plans for Turkish-operated air defence systems to follow.
Israeli officials claimed such a deployment could alter the regional balance of power by limiting Israel's ability to carry out air operations over Syria.
Abu al-Duhur lies around 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Saturday that the military had repeatedly recommended striking the base after receiving what he described as "clear intelligence" about Turkey's plans.
"The army recommended several times carrying out the strike at Abu al-Duhur airport, in light of clear intelligence obtained regarding Turkey's intention to undertake activities there that would endanger the security of the State of Israel," Katz said.
Katz said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior security officials had agreed to warn Damascus before authorising the attack.
"It was agreed that before approval was granted, a direct warning would be sent to the Syrian regime at the highest levels, in an attempt to prevent this move, and that is indeed what happened," he said.
He added that the intelligence had also been shared with Washington.
According to Katz, Damascus failed to act on the warning, prompting Israel to approve the strike.
"Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Israeli officials quoted by Ynet said Ankara had been preparing to install radar at the base before deploying air defence systems and a Turkish commando unit to operate them.
The officials said Israel believes Turkey could attempt a similar deployment elsewhere in Syria in the future.
They also claimed that Turkish-operated air defences in Syria could make any future Israeli strike on Iran more difficult by restricting Israeli aircraft operating in Syrian airspace.
Under international law, Israel has no general right to strike Syrian territory or dictate Damascus's foreign and security relationships. Syria's decision to establish military or political ties with Turkey is a matter of its sovereignty and self-determination, subject to its own international obligations.
The attack comes amid renewed tensions between Israel and Syria despite recent efforts to reach a security arrangement between the two countries.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said last month that Damascus wanted an agreement with Israel that could "pave the way for a comprehensive peace", while insisting Syria would not abandon its claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which is considered illegally occupied and annexed under international law.
Israel also carried out another strike in Syria on Saturday, targeting a vehicle in the town of Beit Jinn in the Damascus countryside.
The Israeli military said it had fired on a person who posed "an immediate threat" to its forces and threatened further attacks against perceived threats.
Reserve Israeli officer Eyal Dror told Ynet that recent developments suggested relations with Syria were moving away from stability.
"In the absence of an attempt to reach some kind of arrangement or settlement, we may see these events with greater frequency," Dror said.

articles.title: Burnham to visit Ukraine with promise of boost for Kyiv’s long-range missiles
articles.body:
Britain will boost Ukraine’s capacity to make its own long-range missiles, Andy Burnham will announce on Monday, as he travels to Kyiv for the country’s independence day on his first foreign visit as prime minister.
Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on Monday morning at a crucial time in the war, with Kyiv braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks and the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, facing his most direct domestic challenge.
The UK prime minister will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version.
While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations.
Burnham said in a statement on Sunday night: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.
“I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.
“The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.
“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”
Burnham will announce in Kyiv that the UK will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month.
Macron spoke to Zelenskyy on Saturday to promise to deliver separate interceptor missiles, which could help counter the recent barrage of high-speed Russian missile attacks on Kyiv.
Meanwhile, European leaders have condemned Friday’s drone attack on a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine, which killed 16 people in Zelenskyy’s home town of Kryvyi Rih.
The Ukrainian military has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors, and the US president, Donald Trump, recently backtracked on a promise to let Ukraine build its own.
However, Zelenskyy said over the weekend he still wanted to buy more US-made Patriots, adding that Ukraine was happy to pay for them rather than receive them as military aid. “I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package,” he said. “The request from our air force is 360.”
He added that he had reached an agreement with France on at least one air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 interceptors in 2027-28.
Macron posted on X on Saturday: “It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression … It is essential that all countries with capabilities at their disposal also join this effort.”
The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years’ time.
But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.
Last week, Russia accused the UK of deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, warning that the deeper Britain’s involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.
This weekend it emerged that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador in London without naming a replacement, prompting speculation it was downgrading its diplomatic presence in the UK.
Burnham has insisted that Russian threats will not weaken British support for Ukraine, saying last week: “We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
The prime minister will on Monday use a meeting of the coalition of the willing, which comprises 34 countries that have promised to help secure Ukraine in the event of a peace deal with Russia, to underline that commitment.
The meeting will be co-chaired by Burnham and Macron, who will join remotely via video link. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, will also take part in the call as the leaders discuss ways to help Ukraine repel the recent wave of long-distance attacks.
While there, Burnham will attend independence day events, the details of which are being kept secret amid concerns of a major Russian attack, and receive an award in recognition of the UK’s support for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy is facing the most concerted internal political challenge of his presidency after the call for an election by his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
The Ukrainian president responded to Fedorov’s dramatic announcement for the first time this weekend, telling reporters on Saturday that holding elections, which have been suspended since the war began, risked splitting the country.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” he said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.
“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he added.

articles.title: EU approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine for air defense, missiles, radars and more
articles.body:
EU approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine for air defense, missiles, radars and more
Kyiv • UNN
On Independence Day, the EU approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine. The funds will be allocated to air defense, missiles, ammunition and radars.
The EU allocated €6.1 billion to Ukraine on Independence Day for air defense and more, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday, UNN reports.
On Ukraine’s Independence Day, we express our unwavering support. Today, we approved €6.1 billion for air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs. Europe is with you today, tomorrow and for as long as necessary
"Happy Independence Day!" the European Commission president congratulated Ukraine in Ukrainian.
The European Commission said that the new approved defense procurements for Ukraine are worth €6.1 billion. "This funding covers air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars, confirming Europe’s commitment to supporting Ukraine’s defense and resilience against Russia’s ongoing aggression," the European Commission said.
The funding, as stated, is part of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (UASL) and is being provided amid Russia’s escalation of ballistic missile and drone attacks. "With 376 missile strikes recorded in July alone, strengthening Ukraine’s defenses is becoming increasingly urgent," the statement said.
Today’s approval of the funding, it was noted, "complements already approved procurement plans worth €16 billion, of which €8.35 billion has already been disbursed, ensuring Ukraine’s timely and necessary receipt of critical supplies."
"The majority of procurements will be made from EU defense companies. In view of Russia’s intensified use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, the European Commission emphasizes the need for a significant increase in deliveries to the EU by drawing down stocks, redirecting orders and scaling up production," the statement said.
"Ukraine’s ability to defend itself depends on the rapid availability of critical defense products. The UASL program provides €30 billion in budget support and €60 billion for defense over 2026–2027, including €28.3 billion in 2026 to strengthen Ukraine’s defense-industrial capacity," the European Commission added.
Next steps
"Ukraine may submit payment requests by providing contracts signed with defense companies. The European Commission will review these contracts before disbursing the funds to ensure that the financial assistance is used for procurements agreed upon with the member states and the European Commission," the European Commission said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy meets US senators: sanctions and ballistic missile defence discussed
articles.body:
Zelenskyy meets US senators: sanctions and ballistic missile defence discussed
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US senators from both parties – Richard Blumenthal and James Lankford – in Kyiv on 23 August.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy thanked the American lawmakers for their unwavering bipartisan and bicameral support, referring to the anti-Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
"We appreciate that work continues in both chambers of the US Congress to increase pressure on Russia, and we hope that Lindsey Graham's bill on sanctions against Russia and Iran can ultimately be passed," he stressed.
Zelenskyy briefed the senators on Russia's constant ballistic missile terror and emphasised that Ukraine must have the capabilities to counter such strikes. According to him, Washington granting licences for Patriot production "could significantly help".
They also discussed cooperation between Ukraine and the US, bilateral agreements and prospective projects.
Background:
- On 7 August, the US Senate approved the sanctions bill against Russia with 86 votes in favour. The bill was co-authored by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham and Democrat Richard Blumenthal. It concerns "punitive" tariffs on countries that import Russian energy resources.
- Further consideration in the House of Representatives and passage are possible no earlier than September – lawmakers are on recess until 31 August.
- US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his wish for the bill to include provisions on Iran but indicated he is prepared to sign it out of respect for the late Graham.

articles.title: Ukraine at 35: Coming of Age Under Fire
articles.body:
Thirty-five years after Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union on Aug. 24, 1991, the country is still fighting for the right to live by that decision. The referendum on Dec. 1, 1991, when more than 90% of Ukrainians backed independence, was supposed to settle the question. Russia’s war has made clear that it did not.
Ukraine at 35 is no longer the hesitant post-Soviet state many expected it to remain. It has built a stronger civic identity, chosen Europe, and learned, at enormous cost, what independence really requires. But the price has been brutal: years of Russian attack, a smaller population, and an economy battered by war and corruption.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The change in how Ukrainians see themselves is hard to miss, and the geopolitical shift has been just as striking. NATO membership, once a marginal idea, now has broad support. The old east-west divides have not disappeared entirely, but they no longer define the country. War has hardened a common sense of fate.
Ukraine has also stopped being treated merely as a space where others act. It has become a country that acts – shaping European security, innovating on the battlefield, and forcing the world to take its choices seriously.
None of this mitigates the damage. Ukraine’s population on government-controlled territory is now roughly 29 million, down from 52 million at independence. Births have fallen, deaths have risen, and millions of Ukrainians are still living abroad.
Ukraine Backers Gather as War Escalates, Air Defense Runs Low
For many families, staying has become a hard calculation: conscription, blackouts and missile strikes at home, or uncertainty in exile. Martial law has delayed elections, testing democratic habits even as Ukrainians continue to demand clean government and accountability.
That democratic reflex remains one of Ukraine’s greatest strengths. Civil society has remained active and defends anti-corruption institutions. Journalists still expose wrongdoing, and citizens still argue fiercely about the country they want to build, even under wartime pressure.
The same is true beyond Ukraine’s borders. The refugee wave has created a larger, more rooted diaspora across Europe and elsewhere. Some 5.6 million Ukrainians remain abroad, and with return intentions leveling off at about 43%, many have begun to build new lives.
That is a loss, but it is also a resource Ukraine cannot afford to waste. Remittances help families survive. Diaspora networks raise aid, lobby governments and can bring back skills, capital and contacts when reconstruction finally begins.
If Ukraine is to recover, it will need both: a stubborn democratic culture at home and a global Ukrainian community that remains tied to the country’s future. It will also need the reforms required for EU membership to move from promise to practice.
Ukraine at 35 has shown that it can resist, adapt and surprise the world. The next task is harder in a different way: to turn courage into institutions, survival into recovery, and independence into something no future Kremlin can overturn. To anchor the country firmly in the democratic world and a reliable security structure and not to let down the friends and allies that have helped Ukraine survive during its darkest days with crucial political, financial and military support.
For Kyiv Post, which has chronicled this struggle through many of its hardest chapters, the anniversary is more than a date on the calendar. It is a marker of how far Ukraine has come, and why its fight matters far beyond its borders.
In 35 years, Ukraine has shown that a post-Russian colony state (tsarist then Soviet) can choose decolonization, democracy, build a civic nation, resist renewed imperial aggression and help reshape the security map of Europe.

articles.title: US tanker aircraft leave Bulgaria as Iran war raises doubts over NATO protection

US tanker aircraft leave Bulgaria as Iran war raises doubts over NATO protection
TEHRAN — Two US Air Force KC-135 tanker aircraft, originally deployed to support US military operations involving Iran, have departed Bulgaria’s Bezmer Air Base. The withdrawal was confirmed on Friday by Bulgaria’s Defense Minister, Dimitar Stoyanov.
The temporary deployment was requested by the United States—which launched a joint military campaign with Israel against Iran on February 28—under a bilateral agreement governing the joint use of military facilities.
On July 22, Bulgaria’s parliament officially authorized the use of Bezmer Air Base as a refueling site, permitting roughly 250 US military personnel to be stationed at the facility until October. However, the decision immediately sparked protests among residents who voiced fears that the presence of the American planes could make the area a target for Iranian missile and drone strikes.
The deployment also triggered swift diplomatic warnings from Tehran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke to his Bulgarian counterpart shortly after the authorization, reminding her that "any party that participates in any way in carrying out a military attack against Iran will certainly have to accept responsibility for its consequences." Earlier in July, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei issued a similar warning against hosting the American aircraft, stating that facilitating such operations would amount to "complicity in the crimes of aggression and war crimes."
Tensions mounted further following a recent report by the Financial Times alleging that Tehran had evaluated potential strikes against American military assets in southeastern Europe—specifically highlighting Bulgaria—if the US escalated the conflict. In response to the report, an unnamed NATO official asserted that the alliance was fully prepared to address any threats against US military targets on European soil.
Dr. Tania Glouhtcheva, PhD in Political Sciences and Head of the International Department at Bulgaria’s DUMA newspaper, shared her insights on the local mood following the departure of the US aircraft. “Of course, people are calm now, especially those living in Bezmer.”
Despite the temporary relief, she raised deeper questions regarding NATO’s security guarantees for the region. “The main concern for most Bulgarians and Europeans is that NATO won’t be able to protect us,” she stated. “Most people don’t believe NATO is as strong as it is portrayed. Although we are part of the EU, crises in recent years have shown that every country acts in its own interests and would rather protect itself than help another member state.”
Dr. Glouhtcheva also expressed skepticism regarding Washington's reliability as a partner for Sofia.
“Although there is a very pro-American party in the parliament, ready to do whatever Trump orders, I think most people retain their common sense,” she said.
Pointing to shiftable geopolitical stances under the US leadership, she added, “Donald Trump changes his mind constantly. Today he assures us he is our friend and ally; tomorrow, he decides the opposite.”
The departure of the KC-135 tankers from Bezmer Air Base has brought immediate relief to local communities that feared being drawn into the crossfire of the West Asia conflict. Yet the episode has exposed far deeper concerns about Europe’s security architecture. For many Bulgarians, the controversy has reinforced doubts over whether NATO can actually shield its members from the consequences of a wider conflict, particularly when US military operations turn European territory into a potential target. It also underscores the difficult position of smaller NATO members, caught between pressure to meet alliance commitments and the growing need to protect their own populations from the risks created by Washington’s military engagements. At the heart of the debate is a growing concern that NATO’s security guarantees may offer less protection than expected, while closer alignment with US military operations could instead leave European allies more exposed to the consequences of conflict.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia could produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, currently has around 600
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia could produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, currently has around 600
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Russia has the potential to produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, and currently has around 600-630 such missiles at its disposal.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists, as reported by Ukrinform
Details: According to Zelenskyy, Russia is aiming to reach a production rate of around 100 ballistic missiles a month, but has not yet achieved that level.
Quote: "I believe Russia could produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year. Now they have 600-630. We have a fairly good understanding of the volume they're aiming for between now and the end of winter.
They could potentially reach around 100 ballistic missiles a month. But they don't have that yet."
Details: Zelenskyy said that the defence forces are working to reduce the capabilities of Russia's military industry, including striking military facilities linked to missile production.
He noted that Ukrainian air defence has become more effective at shooting down Russian cruise missiles thanks to combat aviation, IRIS-T and Hawk air defence systems, though countering ballistic missiles remains more difficult.
The president also said that Ukraine is carrying out specific operations aimed at disrupting preparations for massive Russian missile attacks.
Quote: "I think you've seen recently that at some point they were planning a strike but didn't carry it out.
That's not a coincidence. We're working to prevent them from being able to carry out massive missile attacks."
Details: Zelenskyy added that Ukraine's Armed Forces had struck a Russian Iskander missile system near the Ukrainian border. He did not give an exact date or location.

articles.title: UK PM to announce new support for Ukraine's long-range missile production
articles.body:
UK PM to announce new support for Ukraine's long-range missile production
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will announce during a visit to Kyiv for Ukraine's Independence Day on 24 August that the UK will strengthen Ukraine's ability to produce its own long-range Scalp missiles.
Source: The Guardian, citing the UK government's website
Details: This will be Burnham's first visit to Ukraine since becoming prime minister.
The Guardian noted that Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on the morning of 24 August at a decisive moment in the war, as Kyiv prepares for another wave of Russian missile strikes and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy faces his most serious domestic challenge.
He will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow European defence company MBDA to declassify information about British components used in the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles, helping Ukraine develop its own version.
"The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years' time. But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high," the Guardian noted.
Burnham will also announce that the UK will help France establish long-range missile assembly lines in Ukraine, a move French President Emmanuel Macron promised last month.
The UK announcement is a small step within a much larger, long-term project that could eventually enable Ukraine to produce its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile.
The Guardian suggested that the move is likely to trigger another wave of criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.
Background:
- Last week, Russia accused the UK of deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to carry out attacks using British-made drones, warning that the deeper UK's involvement becomes, "the higher the price it will pay".
- Over the weekend, it emerged that Russia had recalled its ambassador to London without appointing a replacement, prompting speculation that Moscow was reducing its diplomatic presence in the UK.
- Burnham stressed that Russian threats would not weaken UK's support for Ukraine, saying last week: "We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need, and that won't change."
- On 24 August, Burnham will use a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, comprising 34 countries that have pledged to help ensure Ukraine's security in the event of a peace deal with Russia, to underline this commitment.
- The meeting will be chaired by Burnham and Macron, who will join by video link. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will also take part in the online conference, during which leaders will discuss ways to help Ukraine withstand the recent wave of long-range attacks.
- During his stay in Kyiv, Burnham will attend events marking Ukraine's Independence Day, details of which are being kept secret amid fears of a major Russian attack. The UK PM is also expected to receive an award in recognition of his country's support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Pakistan’s rise as a regional mediator could reshape Middle East diplomacy - analysis
articles.body:
Pakistan is increasingly positioning itself as one of the Middle East’s most important diplomatic players.
Over the past week, Islamabad has simultaneously deepened strategic ties with Syria, prepared for high-level talks with Iran, and continued its role as a potential mediator between Tehran and Washington.
In a sense, Pakistan had taken a step back over the last two months. Now it is trying to return to the table. Pakistan is seeking to become an influential actor in shaping the region’s future. This was clear over the last year. The Trump administration has trusted Pakistan and worked with it.
The timing is important. The Middle East remains in transition following the US and Israeli military campaign against Iran that began in late February. While a memorandum of understanding is supposedly in play, tensions continue to grow. Iran is increasing its threat. The US is also talking up new economic pressure.
According to the media site Rudaw, Pakistan’s Army Chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is expected to travel to Tehran as part of Islamabad’s effort to promote “regional stability.” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said the visit is intended to strengthen cooperation while continuing Pakistan’s “good offices” in promoting peace and security.
The announcement followed a telephone conversation between Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who discussed developments and diplomatic efforts. There is a lot of generalized language here. However, what is important is that the visit is happening.
Pakistan’s role has evolved over the last several months. Rudaw noted that Islamabad helped mediate between Iran and the United States after the outbreak of fighting earlier this year, contributing to negotiations that produced a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington.
Pakistan has emerged as a mediator between US and Iran
Although tensions remain, Pakistan has emerged as one of the countries capable of maintaining dialogue with both sides.
That role may become even more important as Washington increases economic pressure on Tehran.
US President Donald Trump recently announced what he described as economic warfare against Iran, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised tough sanctions. Those measures are expected to further tighten restrictions on Iran’s economy and increase pressure on countries that continue commercial ties with Tehran.
Iran has responded with new threats. Iran feels confident it can outfox the Americans.
According to a second Rudaw report, Mohsen Rezai, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned neighboring countries against cooperating with the new American sanctions campaign.
Rezai stated that if the economic blockade continued, Iran would prevent Gulf oil exports from leaving the region. “If the blockade continues, we will not allow a single drop of Persian Gulf oil to leave via any route,” Rezai said in remarks carried by Iranian state TV.
He also noted that Iran could target American economic interests if pressure continued, while insisting that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until Washington changed its policies. Iran is showcasing its continued arrogance.
These comments illustrate how the confrontation between the US and Iran has shifted. Earlier phases centered on military conflict: Missile strikes, drone attacks, and military operations. Now the competition is taking place through sanctions, maritime pressure, and competing trade routes. Each side wants to see who will blink first. Hormuz remains important to that struggle because roughly 20% of global oil shipments previously transited the waterway before the conflict disrupted maritime commerce.
Pakistan FM’s Syria visit highlights expanding regional partnerships
Pakistan is expanding its regional partnerships elsewhere. According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani recently concluded the first visit by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan in 19 years.
The visit reflects Damascus’s broader effort to rebuild regional relationships following the fall of the Assad regime and to establish what Syrian officials described as a “new Syrian state.”
During meetings with Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Army Chief Asim Munir, and other senior officials, the two countries discussed expanding cooperation in politics, security, trade, aviation, and investment. Syria welcomed the recently announced Mecca Agreement for Mutual Defense and praised Pakistan’s role in supporting regional stability.
SANA reported that the two governments also discussed investment forums, restoring direct flights, and coordinating on regional diplomacy, including Pakistan’s efforts to reduce tensions between Iran and the US.
Syrian officials emphasized that Pakistan now sits alongside Saudi Arabia and Turkey as one of Syria’s strategic partners.
Mohammad al-Jaffal, an adviser at Syria’s Foreign Ministry, said relations with Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad represent three complementary tracks designed to strengthen Syria’s regional role. This could lead to Syria joining the new alliance of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, which would raise eyebrows in Israel, where tensions are growing with Turkey.
Pakistan emerging as a bridge between multiple countries
Taken together, these developments point toward Pakistan becoming a bridge between multiple countries. Islamabad maintains longstanding defense cooperation with Saudi Arabia. It has steadily expanded military and industrial cooperation with Turkey. It is now rebuilding relations with Syria while preserving dialogue with Iran and maintaining working ties with Washington.
For the US, Pakistan’s expanding regional role presents many opportunities. Islamabad’s ability to communicate with Tehran, Damascus, Riyadh, Ankara, and Washington could prove valuable during the next crisis.
Pakistan must be careful, though. It has to show the Trump administration it can achieve results. The administration now wants to see things happen that can help the US wind down this conflict. At the same time, balancing those relationships will become increasingly difficult if conflict between Iran and the US continues to grow.
The coming weeks will provide an early indication of whether Pakistan can successfully maintain its role as a regional mediator while also expanding its strategic initiatives.

articles.title: Iran shifts to offensive posture
articles.body:
Iran shifts to offensive posture
Major General Mohsen Rezaei warns Iran will target the interests of countries joining the US economic war
TEHRAN — Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the newly appointed Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), warned on Saturday that the Islamic Republic will respond decisively to any country joining Washington’s economic warfare against the nation.
“We will neutralize the economic war. America is backed into a corner. Either they honor their commitments, or they will have to struggle to get out of that corner, which will make the situation worse,” General Rezaei said during a televised interview.
Rezaei’s warning came after US President Donald Trump threatened a campaign of economic coercion against Iran while issuing illegal threats of secondary sanctions against any nation maintaining legitimate commercial ties with Tehran. “We tell all neighboring countries not to enter the economic war against Iran. Anyone who does so will be considered a hostile country,” General Rezaei said, adding, “First, we will negotiate with them and ask them not to do this; if they continue, we will target interests of that country.”
Following the unprovoked illegal US-Israeli military aggression launched on February 28, which targeted Iranian infrastructure, the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic forced the hostile coalition into a desperate retreat, culminating in the April 8 ceasefire and the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU). However, in blatant defiance of international law, Washington reneged on its signed commitments. Having suffered a crushing defeat on the battlefield, Trump has now resorted to a desperate campaign of sanctions—arrogantly dubbed "Economic D-Day"—in a futile attempt to cover up Washington’s failed military strategy against the Iranian nation.
Further in his remarks, Rezaei stressed that Iran holds the military capability to prevent oil from passing through the entire Persian Gulf if such hostile measures are pursued. “If they start such an action, we will not allow a single drop of oil to pass through the Persian Gulf. Oil will leave neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor through the Persian Gulf. For now, we have closed the Strait of Hormuz, while we are not targeting the oil in the Persian Gulf,” the SNSC secretary said.
The top security official, meanwhile, ruled out any immediate reopening of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, emphasizing that Washington must first take concrete, verifiable steps to honor its previous commitments. He pointed to an agreement between Iran and Oman regarding the maritime pass. “This commercial route is shared by Iran and Oman.” He added, “There is another identity here that belongs to us. The Strait of Hormuz is the gateway into the Persian Gulf, and Oman has no presence inside the Persian Gulf proper. Therefore, we cannot relinquish our rightful control over the Strait of Hormuz.”
Rezaei explained that Iran’s defense strategy and diplomatic conduct have fundamentally transformed in response to the recent American-Israeli military aggression and Iran’s determined retaliatory closure of the strait. “Iran today will not be the Iran it was before the war. Of course, the overconfident United States is not the same America it was before the war either. Iran’s patterns of behavior in the international arena have transformed. The entire world now looks at us differently, and we have no choice but to evolve our behavior in this context.”
According to Rezaei, Iran will incorporate key strategic lessons from the conflict into its future defense planning, continuing to advance indigenously developed technologies while adjusting its diplomatic posture in response to persistent US violations. “The Leader’s decision to bring in experienced commanders means that we will certainly apply the lessons we have learned in the next battle,” the official noted, referring to Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei’s recent appointment of veteran commanders to key military positions, including Rezaei himself. “Certainly, changes will be made in the way Iran manages and conducts war, as well as in its diplomatic conduct. The reason is clear: The Americans betrayed the negotiations and reneged on their own signature.”
Rezaei characterized Washington's current approach as a weak attempt to rely on economic pressure after its military tactics failed on the ground. He dismissed the economic measures as mere media propaganda, noting that Iranian trade remains active despite illegal blockades. “Take the issue of the American naval blockade. This is not something new. In the past one or two months alone, we have successfully shipped 70 million barrels of oil.” Despite the warnings, Rezaei affirmed that Iran remains committed to genuine diplomacy, while stressing that Tehran will pursue negotiation from a position of absolute strength.
“We are serious about diplomacy, but we have changed our method… We are waiting for the other side to honor its commitments. We want the wars in Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, and Yemen to end,” the security chief said, emphasizing the Islamic Republic’s unwavering demand for an immediate end to regional aggression across all fronts.
Rezaei reaffirmed that while the Islamic Republic does not seek conflict, it will defend its sovereignty without hesitation. “We are not warmongers, but we will never surrender. We will sacrifice every last drop of our blood for the people and Iran.” “We advise the Americans not to increase their forces; if they do, we will strike them. Every meeting they hold with counter-revolutionary elements, we will strike. Our attacks are now precisely targeted.”
New geopolitical reality
The bluster emanating from the White House regarding an "economic D-Day" is not a sign of American strength, but rather the unmistakable death rattle of a failing imperial strategy. By turning to financial terrorism after the failure of its direct military aggression alongside Israel, Washington has conceded a pivotal truth: the United States and its regional vassals cannot dictate terms to the Islamic Republic through force of arms.
The military conflict that began with the illegal US-Israeli attacks on February 28 exposed the severe vulnerabilities of Western power. For decades, Pentagon strategists operated under the illusion that overwhelming airpower and naval presence could force Tehran into capitulation. Instead, Iran's sophisticated asymmetric defense doctrine, precision ballistic strikes, and advanced drone technology shattered enemy formations, inflicting unprecedented strategic costs and forcing the aggressors to sue for the April 8 ceasefire. When the June 17 memorandum of understanding was signed, it served as formal recognition of Iran's victory on the battlefield and its undisputed status as the preeminent power in West Asia. However, Washington’s habitual treachery—manifested in its immediate violation of the June 17 agreement—surprised no one in Tehran. Trump’s reliance on coercive sanctions is a rehashed tactic from a bygone era. The global economic landscape is no longer subservient to Western dictation.
Over the past decade, Iran has systematically fortified its economic resilience, developing sophisticated trade networks, alternative financial corridors, and robust bilateral mechanisms with non-Western powers. The fact that Iran successfully exported tens of millions of barrels of oil in recent weeks under the nose of an aggressive American blockade stands as living proof that the era of Western economic hegemony has reached its end.
Furthermore, Major General Rezaei’s firm message to neighboring states underscores a critical shift in regional dynamics. Foreign military bases and economic compliance with hostile powers are no longer cost-free propositions for regional capitals. The Persian Gulf is the historic domain of the nations that border it, and any attempt by regional actors to facilitate Washington's economic aggression will be met with swift, decisive retaliatory measures. By holding complete leverage over the Strait of Hormuz—the vital artery of international energy markets—Tehran possesses the absolute capability to turn any illegal economic blockade against the aggressors themselves.  Under the guidance of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, and reinforced by battlefield-tested leadership across the Supreme National Security Council and Armed Forces, Iran’s defense and diplomatic posture has evolved permanently. The era of unilateral Western concessions is over. Tehran will no longer negotiate under duress or tolerate broken promises. If the United States wishes to prevent complete economic chaos and further military humiliation, it must abandon its arrogant dictates, recognize its defeat, and honor every obligation it has repeatedly signed and betrayed.

Live Updates: U.S. Treasury to unveil new Iran sanctions after Trump warned of "economic D-Day" for Tehran
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will unveil new sanctions against Iran on Monday that he described as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary." The move is part of a strategy shift to pile economic pressure on the Islamic republic in the hope of breaking the stalemate between the two countries.
- Talks between Iran and Oman on the future management of the Strait of Hormuz are set to continue on Tuesday. The two countries have been negotiating for weeks about how to manage the traffic of ships through the vital waterway, with suggestions of fees and specific routes emerging as possible solutions.
- Iran's president said Sunday that he believes the memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and his country is still the best path forward to ending the war. The agreement was signed in June and called for a 60-day negotiation period. That deadline has since expired and both countries have previously declared the deal to be dead.
Ship struck off the coast of Saudi Arabia
A ship was struck by an unknown projectile in the Red Sea off the coast of Saudi Arabia, the British military's Maritime Trade Operations agency said Monday.
The incident caused a fire on the main deck of the vessel, but the crew was safe, UKMTO said in a brief statement.
The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported.
Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels said on July 20 that they would impose a blockade on Saudi ports and vessels in the Red Sea, and they have since attacked multiple Saudi-owned tankers in the region.
Greek military reportedly moves Patriot interceptor systems in response to Iranian threats
The Greek military on Monday moved one of its Patriot missile interceptor systems to the island of Crete in response to Iranian threats to hit U.S. military bases in Europe, local media reports said.
The battery was moved from the eastern island of Karpathos to Crete, where there is a major U.S. base at Souda, the reports said. Media images showed the Patriot system on a truck waiting to be loaded on a barge.
The Financial Times reported last week, quoting Iranian sources, that Iran would fire missiles at U.S. targets in Europe if President Donald Trump steps up military pressure over the Strait of Hormuz.
The Greek defence ministry did not comment on the reported transfer of the missile system.
Iran-Oman talks on Strait of Hormuz to continue Tuesday
Oman and Iran are set to continue their talks on the future management of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Tehran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday.
The spokesperson said Oman's foreign minister will travel to Tehran to meet with Iranian officials.
The two countries, whose shorelines include the strategic waterway, have been engaged in talks for weeks to negotiate how to manage the chokepoint. Some details have emerged regarding the possible introduction of fees for ships transiting the strait, as well as specific routes for entering and exiting the area.
CBS/AFP
Treasury Secretary warns Iran, allies of "economic D-Day"
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned Iran and its allies the U.S. will unleash an "economic D-Day" on Iran as part of a shift in strategy to pile economic pressure in the hope of breaking the stalemate in the conflict – a term first used by President Trump last week.
Writing in the British Financial Times newspaper, Bessent said the measures would be the "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary."
The secretary also urged Iran's allies to sever ties with Tehran, saying that doing so would "deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy."
Bessent is set to hold a news conference on Monday at which he will unveil the new measures.
After months of military pressure and a failed agreement to negotiate an end to the war, Mr. Trump signaled in recent weeks a shift in the strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.
Iran's president defends memorandum of understanding as best path forward
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended the memorandum of understanding signed with the U.S. in June as the best way for the country to move beyond what he described as a situation of "neither war nor peace."
In a speech published by state-run IRNA news agency Sunday, he said members of Iran's Supreme National Security Council believed the agreement was the best possible based on what he described as dignity, wisdom and the national interest.
"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."
The deal known as the Memorandum of Understanding was signed by President Trump in June. It set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war with Iran and reaching an accord on its nuclear program. That period ended last week, after weeks of months of stalled progress and flare-ups, with both sides declaring they had abandoned it.. There appear to be no signs of compromise on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global shipping.
CBS/AP
Iran says any country joining U.S. sanctions is considered an "enemy"
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' "economic war" against the Islamic republic, saying they would be considered enemies.
"We declare to all countries ... do not join the economic war waged by the United States. Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran's supreme national security council, said on state television.
If the countries concerned refuse to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.
Rezai also insisted Iran had more cards to play in the war, claiming, "We have not yet attacked any American economic interests."
President Trump said last week the U.S. will enforce "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale." But he also called on the rest of the world to come to the aid of the U.S. in enforcing sanctions, the specifics of which have still not been announced.
CBS/AFP

articles.title: Denmark to continue providing military aid to Ukraine, PM says
articles.body:
Denmark to continue providing military aid to Ukraine, PM says
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said this during her speech at a ceremony to raise Ukraine’s National Flag, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
Addressing Ukrainians, the Danish Prime Minister stressed that defending Kharkiv and Odesa also means defending Riga, Helsinki, and Copenhagen
“Denmark and the Nordic and Baltic countries stand with you. From the very beginning, we knew that this war could not be won with words alone. When you urgently needed weapons and ammunition, we provided them. When you needed tanks and our F-16s, we provided them. When you needed investment in your own defense industry, we provided it. And now, when you are in urgent need of strong air defense, we must promise to provide it,” Frederiksen said.
She recalled that Denmark and other countries had jointly committed to rapidly developing a new missile system to protect Ukrainian cities and strengthen Europe’s defenses.
“Our support cannot be measured in money. It can be measured by one simple promise: for as long as it takes,” the Danish Prime Minister assured.
As reported, on Sunday, August 23, Ukraine is celebrating National Flag Day. In addition to Denmark’s Prime Minister, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, President of Lithuania Gitanas Nausėda, Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Støre, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, and Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs arrived in Kyiv.

articles.title: UK's PM Burnham to visit Ukraine with plan to support long-range missile production
articles.body:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Ukraine on Monday on his first overseas trip since taking office, and will announce British support to help Kyiv improve its domestic production of long-range missiles.
Burnham will be in Ukraine to co-chair a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries backing Ukraine, on Monday when he is also due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
He is set to announce that Britain has agreed to allow European missile manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on British-made components used in the SCALP long-range cruise missile, according to his office.
That will help enable France and Ukraine to establish local assembly lines for the missile, which shares British and French technology, according to Downing Street.
"Ukraine's security is our security," Burnham said in a statement, adding that Britain would stand by Ukraine "for as long as it takes."
Britain has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, providing military support, economic aid and diplomatic backing.
Britain was the first country to announce plans to supply Ukraine with Western-made battle tanks and long-range cruise missiles following the invasion and has pledged more than £25 billion so far in military and civilian support.
Reassurance of UK support for Ukraine
Moscow warned London last week of "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv, accusing Britain of deepening its involvement in the war following a report that British-made drones had been used for long-range strikes against Russia for the first time.
Burnham is expected to use his visit to reassure Ukraine and its allies that Britain would continue to play a leading role in efforts to strengthen Ukraine's security under his government.
The push to expand Ukraine's domestic missile production comes as Ukraine increasingly relies on long-range drones and strike weapons to target Russian oil refineries and logistics facilities far behind the front lines.
The visit comes weeks after Zelensky traveled to Britain in late July as Burnham's first international guest, following the Labour leader's election as prime minister a week earlier.

articles.title: Syria says US-mediated talks addressed de-escalation, staying out of Israel-Turkey tensions
articles.body:
Syria says US-mediated talks addressed de-escalation, staying out of Israel-Turkey tensions
Syria and Israel held US-mediated talks in Jordan on Sunday to defuse the crisis sparked by a strike that Israel said was aimed at preventing a Turkish military deployment. Damascus says it wants to stay out of the tensions between Israel and Turkey.
Syria said it held US-mediated talks with Israel in Jordan on Sunday focusing on de-escalation after recent Israeli strikes, and on keeping the country out of tensions between Israel and Turkey, an ally of Damascus.
The high-level negotiations came after the sides in January agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism as they edge towards a security agreement.
They also came after Israel bombed the disused Abu Duhur airbase in the country's northwest earlier in the week, claiming it wanted to avert Turkish troops deploying to the facility. Ankara denied any visit to the site.
Read moreIsrael says strikes on Syrian military airfield were to ensure its security
Syrian state news agency SANA quoted a diplomatic source at the foreign ministry saying "a high-level Syrian delegation headed by the foreign minister and including the general and military intelligence chiefs" met a high-level Israeli delegation "under American mediation and hosted by Jordan".
The meeting was "part of efforts aiming at de-escalation after recent Israeli bombardment of Syrian territory, escalating tensions in southern Syria, and in support of stability in Syria and the region", said the source.
Discussions also addressed "efforts aimed at bringing closer the viewpoints between Turkey and Israel and ensuring the current tension between the two countries are not reflected on Syria territory", the report added.
A diplomatic source and a Syrian government source told AFP that Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani met the head of Israel's Mossad intelligence agency Roman Gofman.
They discussed issues such as establishing "a special operations room" in Jordan under US supervision to prevent any confrontation in Syria, including involving Turkey, the sources added.
Negotiations
US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack had slammed Israel's attack on the airbase on Tuesday as an "unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability".
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders.
The Syrian government source told AFP that Sunday's talks were the first between Israel and Syria in some time, while the diplomatic source said they were the first in several months.
SANA said the discussions addressed "establishing practical mechanisms to stop Israeli attacks ... and reviving the negotiations process with the aim of reaching a security agreement that could form the basis of a more comprehensive future agreement".
Israel and Syria's new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks, and after negotiations in Paris in January they agreed to establish a dedicated communication cell under US supervision to lower bilateral tensions.
An Arab diplomat in Damascus told AFP at the time that a joint operations room based in Jordan would follow issues including security coordination and border control.
Southern Syria
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the December 2024 toppling of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad by Islamist forces it considers jihadists.
It sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces on the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights.
Read moreSyria slams new Israeli incursion in southern Daraa province
Israel has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
The talks also came a day after Israel struck what it said was a militant in southern Syria. Damascus said one person was wounded in the strike, which it called a "flagrant violation" of its sovereignty.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, a move only recognised by the United States and, this month, Colombia.
US President Donald Trump has been pushing for a security deal between Syria and Israel, but Israel remains distrustful of Syria's authorities.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

General Staff reported 231 engagements in a day: the two hottest fronts
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past day, there were 231 combat engagements, including 35 on the Kostiantynivka front and 20 on the Pokrovsk front. Russia carried out 95 airstrikes and 3,110 shelling attacks.
Up to a quarter of the 231 battles on the front over the past day took place in two directions — Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported in its morning briefing on August 24, UNN writes.
A total of 231 combat engagements were recorded over the past day
Yesterday, the aggressor carried out 95 airstrikes using 299 guided aerial bombs, deployed 10,747 kamikaze drones for attacks, and carried out 3,110 shelling attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas, including 29 using multiple launch rocket systems.

Situation by direction

In the Oleksandrivka direction, the invaders carried out one attack toward Novе Zaporizhzhia.
