In the Dnipro direction, the enemy conducted no offensive actions.
In the Volyn and Polissia directions, no signs of the formation of enemy offensive groups were detected.

articles.title: Germany’s establishment has a plan to contain the far right. Sort of.
articles.body:
Ulrich Siegmund walks past election campaign placards at the Alternative for Germany campaign launch for state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, on June 4, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — It’s not the kind of photo op German Chancellor Friedrich Merz would likely want to frame for his office wall: him standing next to Ulrich Siegmund, the far-right politician a national magazine recently labeled the country’s “most dangerous man.”
And yet, such a picture might soon be hard for Merz to avoid. On Sept. 6, Siegmund is set for a sweeping victory in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. If his far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secures an outright majority in the state parliament, Siegmund will likely become premier, and his party will have broken through the political “firewall” that has kept it out of all federal and state governments since its founding in 2013.
It would be a historic triumph for the AfD and a shock to Germany’s political system.
Advertisement
As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press.
Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said.
The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support.
So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD?
POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name.
The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it. State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record.
Advertisement
The conversations for this article were dominated by a single concern: domestic security, especially the protection of intelligence information, given the AfD’s advocacy for closer ties with President Vladimir Putin’s Russia.
According to Social Democrat Georg Maier, who serves as the state of Thuringia’s interior minister, Siegmund’s party has “good channels” to Moscow. “If the AfD provides the minister-president in Saxony-Anhalt, the champagne corks will be popping in the Kremlin,” he told POLITICO.
AfD supporters listen to Siegmund during a campaign event in Dessau-Roßlau, Germany, on Aug. 19, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Although there is no playbook yet for containing an AfD government, the thinking in Berlin and several state capitals has already moved well beyond the abstract.
Option 1: Hold extra informal meetings
One way to limit the AfD’s access to sensitive discussions could be to simply have more discussions. In addition to the gathering of state premiers that Siegmund would be expected to chair for a year, Germany’s states regularly coordinate through a network of ministerial “conferences.” Among the most important is the conference of interior ministers, where some of the country’s most pressing security and intelligence matters are discussed.
One possibility being considered is to keep holding the regular meetings of the interior ministers but also organize separate gatherings for particularly sensitive issues. Only Germany’s 15 other interior ministers would attend these meetings, without the representative from Saxony-Anhalt. Several ministers confirmed this hypothetical scenario to POLITICO.
The idea builds on a long-established practice in German politics. State governments are informally grouped into so-called “A” and “B” states, depending on which political camp holds the governing majority: Social Democratic-led governments on one side, conservative governments on the other. Before major conferences, both camps coordinate internally.
Advertisement
Applied to the AfD, this model would put the ostracized government on one side and everyone else on the other.
Christoph Degenhart, a professor emeritus of constitutional law and former judge at Saxony’s Constitutional Court, said the idea is definitely conceivable. “How long that would work and whether the courts would tolerate it is, of course, another question.”
Option 2: Erect a wall
One of the biggest worries regarding the AfD is its closeness to Moscow, according to Maier.
Specifically, the minister’s biggest concern is an AfD-led interior ministry. Whoever runs such a department, he said, gains access to highly classified information. And yet, excluding the entire state from Germany’s domestic intelligence network would not be possible; public safety, including protection against terrorist attacks, would rule that out.
“But we can build Chinese walls into our joint information systems, barriers that block certain information,” said the minister. He laughed briefly. “‘Chinese walls’ fits perfectly here. The AfD doesn’t just have a soft spot for Moscow,” he added.
What information would Maier wall off? “We would have to keep all intelligence relating to right-wing extremism and the entire area of espionage away from the AfD,” he said. Such a “preventive segmentation” would be legally possible, he added, citing legal advice he has obtained. It could also be implemented relatively quickly. “Government formation is not going to happen overnight,” he said.
Advertisement
Patrick Harr, a spokesperson for the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, rejected all accusations of closeness to Russia. “That’s complete nonsense,” he said. “We don’t have a red telephone to Moscow.”
“We talk to everyone, whether West or East,” he added. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to hand over files. Anyone who claims otherwise is talking nonsense. If and when we get access to such information, we understand our responsibility as a party of government.”
But Konstantin von Notz, a Green member of the Bundestag and deputy chair of its intelligence oversight panel, pointed to Austria’s far-right Freedom Party’s (FPÖ) time in government as a cautionary example. After entering government in 2017, the FPÖ took control of the interior ministry. The following year, police raided Austria’s domestic intelligence service and seized sensitive data, including information from allied agencies.
Thorsten Frei, right, Friedrich Merz, center, and Markus Söder, left, speak to media in Berlin on July 29, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Germany could face something similar under an AfD government, said von Notz, if for example the country’s allies suspected Russia would be able to access the database used by Germany’s domestic intelligence services to exchange information on extremists, spies and other security threats.
“The British, the Americans, the Poles, the Ukrainians — nobody would share information with us anymore for fear that everything would be passed on to Moscow,” warned the Green politician.
Advertisement
Option 3: Cut off their funds
Another instrument mentioned both by AfD figures and the party’s opponents is Germany’s fiscal equalization system, which helps poorer states with money from wealthier ones and additional federal funds.
Saxony-Anhalt has depended on this system for decades. In 2025, it received around €2.8 billion according to preliminary figures — nearly one-fifth of its state budget.
Reducing or even halting such payments would be one way to make life harder for an AfD government, or to coerce the party to behave in ways the political establishment finds acceptable. Within the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, this scenario is seen as a real risk.
The legal hurdles, however, would be high. Danyal Bayaz, the Green finance minister of Baden-Württemberg, one of Germany’s wealthier contributor states, chose his words carefully. “The fiscal equalization system is anchored in the constitution and is not an instrument that can simply be changed according to the political weather,” he said.
He then added a caveat: A federal state based on solidarity, said Bayaz, depends on shared commitments to the rule of law. If a state government were to call those principles into question, or pursue legally dubious special paths, that would affect trust and cooperation with the federal government and other states, “including in financial matters.”
Bayaz’s spokesperson stressesdthat this was the minister’s personal assessment, not an agreed position of the state government — a coalition led by the Greens, with the CDU as its junior partner.
Advertisement
Option 4: Deploy the nuclear option
The most powerful constitutional instrument would be Bundeszwang, or federal coercion. Under Article 37 of Germany’s Basic Law, the federal government, with the consent of the Bundesrat — the chamber representing the states — may take “necessary measures” to compel a state to fulfill its legal obligations. In plain English: Berlin could force a state government to obey federal law.
The provision has never been used. In the reporting for this story, no one interviewed brought it up on their own — perhaps out of conviction, perhaps out of fear that merely mentioning it would play into the AfD’s hands before the elections.
Within AfD’s right-wing intellectual circles, federal coercion has long been treated as a realistic scenario. In 2025, publisher Götz Kubitschek, whose estate lies in Saxony-Anhalt and who the New York Times once labeled “the prophet of Germany’s new right,” told POLITICO this is what he would expect to see happen.
The entrance to the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Cologne, Germany is pictured on Sept. 22, 2025. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images
A potential trigger can only be guessed at. If, for example, an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt failed to provide for even the most basic needs of asylum seekers, the federal government could intervene with binding orders to restore those services, eventually through a federal commissioner with the authority to issue instructions to the state and all its authorities.
Would all this work?
Whatever Germany’s political establishment does to contain the country’s first AfD government, this fall or later, the risks are obvious. Measures meant to defend liberal democracy could also feed the AfD’s central grievance and that of many of its voters: that the establishment refuses to accept the party even when it wins.
Public opinion on this is more divided than it once was. A representative poll from July found that only 42 percent of Germans still considered it right for the Social Democrats and the CDU to refuse cooperation with the AfD; another survey showed that support for the exclusion strategy had fallen to 46 percent, down from 54 percent in early 2025.
Advertisement
Doing nothing out of the ordinary may well be the safest option for established parties. The AfD has spent years thriving in opposition, turning its rivals’ mistakes and broken promises into political fuel. But it has never governed. Once in office, it could become mired in incompetence and internal infighting, sparing its opponents the need for special defensive maneuvers.
Key figures in the AfD’s own orbit are aware of this danger. “They have to prepare like the biggest overachievers,” Kubitschek told POLITICO in 2025 regarding Siegmund’s state party. Benedikt Kaiser, another influential far-right intellectual and aide to an AfD member of the Bundestag, also advised caution if the party wins an outright majority: “In the first 90 days of government, the AfD has to pursue a politics that does not create fear,” he said, mentioning “family benefits, free school meals, things like that” as examples.
Even as Germany’s political establishment considers ways to contain an AfD state government, the party’s intellectual leaders are fretting over a more immediate concern: Simply governing could prove a more effective constraint on the party than any measure the country’s political mainstream can devise.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 8 missiles and 143 drones - three missiles, including "Oniks," and 111 drones, including "Banderol", neutralized
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 8 missiles and 143 drones - three missiles, including "Oniks," and 111 drones, including "Banderol", neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
Air defense destroyed or suppressed 109 drones, three missiles, and two "Banderol" drones. Hits were recorded at 22 locations.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 8 missiles, including two Oniks, and 143 drones; one Oniks and two other missiles, as well as 109 drones and two Banderols, were shot down or suppressed, the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force reported on Monday, writes UNN.
Details
According to the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force, during the night of August 24 (from 18:00 on August 23), the enemy attacked with two Oniks anti-ship missiles from the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, 6 Kh-31P and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles from the airspace over the Black Sea, as well as 143 Shahed-type attack UAVs (one-third of them jet-powered), Gerbera, S8000 "Banderol" and "Parody"-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Millerovo, Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
"The main direction of the strike was Odesa region," the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force stated.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down/suppressed an Oniks anti-ship missile, 2 Kh-31P and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, and 2 S8000 "Banderol" drones, as well as 109 enemy Shahed- and Gerbera-type UAVs and drones of other types in the south, north and east of the country. Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 22 locations, as well as the falls of downed targets (debris) at 5 locations. In addition, some enemy missiles did not reach their targets; information regarding them is being clarified
The attack, as stated, is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Ozon Warehouses for Third Straight Night
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck at least three Ozon logistics centers and several other sites across southern Russia and occupied Crimea overnight Aug.23-24 – the third consecutive night of strikes on the retail giant
The strikes coincided with Ukraine’s Independence Day, marking 35 years since the country declared independence from the Soviet Union.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A facility in Krasnodar belonging to home goods retailer Kuchenland caught fire during the attack, according to independent Russian Telegram channel Astra.
Krasnodar Krai Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said falling drone debris struck a childcare center, killing two children and injuring seven more along with two adults. He said debris also fell on residential buildings and apartment blocks under construction, and that the strikes sparked a fire at warehouse facilities in the region.
Krasnodar sits roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) from occupied Berdiansk in southeastern Ukraine and about 365 kilometers (227 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory near Orikhiv.
Elsewhere, an Ozon logistics center near the village of Enem in the Adygea Republic was also struck, according to Telegram channel Exile Plus. Another Ozon hub in Nevinnomyssk, in Stavropol Krai, caught fire after being hit, Telegram channel Exilenova Plus reported. Stavropol Krai Governor Vladimir Vladimirov confirmed drones targeted Nevinnomyssk’s industrial zone and said some were intercepted by air defenses, though he did not specify which facilities were targeted.
Kazakhstan Holds Early Elections for New Parliament
A third Ozon site, in the town of Tyube in the Dagestan Republic, was also engulfed in flames after being struck, Exilenova Plus reported.
In occupied Crimea, a fire broke out at a radar tracking unit after four strikes in the area, according to the pro-Ukrainian Telegram channel Crimean Wind.
None of the reports from Russian or Crimean channels could be independently verified.
Monday’s strikes extend a campaign that has intensified in recent days. Ozon logistics centers in Samara Oblast were struck Aug. 22, and another hub in Orenburg was hit overnight Aug. 23.
The broader campaign began weeks ago with Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, which Kyiv accuses of supplying components to the Russian military. On Aug. 16, Ukrainian forces announced that operations had disabled seven of the 10 largest logistics centers belonging to Wildberries.
Ozon and Wildberries, often called “Russia’s Amazon,” dominate the country’s fast-growing e-commerce sector. Their warehouses have become recurring targets, costing Russian businesses – and the Russian war machine – billions of dollars, Ukrainian officials say.

articles.title: Iranian artists to showcase works at Sydney exhibition on war and peace
articles.body:
Iranian artists to showcase works at Sydney exhibition on war and peace
TEHRAN- The Benevolent Iranian Women Association will participate in an art exhibition in Sydney, Australia, in early September, presenting selected works by Iranian artists at an event exploring the human consequences of war and destruction.
The association is taking part in the exhibition, titled “When the Earth Embraces the Sky,” at the invitation of Conference of Birds – Shia Hub for Art & Culture of Sydney.
The exhibition, scheduled to run from September 5 to 13, seeks to portray life in Middle Eastern countries before the outbreak of wars and examine the realities faced by people in the aftermath of conflict and destruction.
According to the organizers, the event aims to draw attention to the devastating consequences of war, humanitarian tragedies, war crimes committed in residential areas, and the killing of innocent civilians.
The Iran section of the exhibition will focus on the Minab school massacre as its central theme, highlighting the human cost of attacks that affect civilian and educational spaces.
The Benevolent Iranian Women Association has invited Iranian artists to submit their works for consideration in the exhibition. Artists are requested to send their works to the email address provided in the official announcement or to the email address designated by the association.
The deadline for submissions is September 2, while the exhibition will be held from September 5 to 13.
Cash prizes will also be awarded to three outstanding artworks selected for the exhibition.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.

articles.title: Ukraine Sought Trump’s Approval to Use Starlink on Russian Territory, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Sought Trump’s Approval to Use Starlink on Russian Territory, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine had sought US political approval to use Starlink on Russian territory for defense purposes after receiving information that SpaceX had initially agreed to such use, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during the meeting with press on August 22.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry approached him in the first half of 2026 and asked him to discuss the issue directly with US President Donald Trump.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In the first half of this year, I received a request from Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense to find an opportunity to reach an agreement with President Trump on the use of Starlink on the territory of the Russian Federation for the purposes of our defense,” Zelenskyy said.
He said he had been informed that SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, had apparently already approved the proposal and that political-level authorization was still required.
The Ukrainian president stated he subsequently raised the issue during a meeting with Trump and argued that expanding Starlink access could help bring the war closer to an end by reducing Russia’s ability to sustain it.
“I am grateful to the President of America—we had a long conversation on this topic. I was able to assure him that this would help bring the end of the war closer by correspondingly reducing Russia’s ability to prolong the war,” Zelenskyy said.
The two sides subsequently agreed that Washington would hold internal discussions on the proposal if SpaceX was prepared to proceed. Zelenskyy said implementing the plan would require more than $1 billion in funding, which he later discussed with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.
However, Zelenskyy said the situation changed by the time of his second meeting with Trump. According to the Ukrainian president, Trump told him that Musk had refused to allow Ukraine to use Starlink on Russian territory.
“He said that I had supposedly deceived him because Musk had refused Ukraine the use of Starlink on Russian territory. I went back to our Ministry of Defense, and they said that perhaps that was indeed the case,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said he was subsequently told that Musk regarded such use of Starlink as potentially constituting a major escalation against Russia.
“As far as we know, Elon Musk believed that this could be a major escalation by Ukraine against the Russian Federation—that is how it was explained to me. He said that he was in favor of stopping the war, not continuing it. We are also in favor of stopping the war, not continuing it, but this requires the appropriate tools,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian drones commonly known as “Starlink planes” are currently limited to operations within Ukrainian territory. Extending Starlink coverage could expand their operational range and allow them to conduct missions deeper inside Russia.
Under the proposal, Ukrainian UAVs relying on Starlink for connectivity and control could reach and strike Russian military targets at greater distances. Ukraine maintains that expanding these capabilities would help target infrastructure used to support Russian attacks farther from its borders.
The Ukrainian president stressed that the information he initially received from the Defense Ministry had differed from what Trump later told him about SpaceX’s position.
Despite the disagreement, Zelenskyy said discussions with Trump and the US administration remain ongoing, although the outcome is difficult to predict.
“It is important that we are now in dialogue with President Trump and the American side, but it is difficult to predict how things will develop—we are working. Today, all of this is on the side of the US president, and they already have their own internal discussions,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy added that several European leaders had also advocated for the proposal with Trump. He said French President Emmanuel Macron raised the issue during a meeting with the US president in Versailles and sought to explain how the plan could contribute to ending the war.
“Emmanuel did everything to explain our idea and how it could bring the end of the war closer, and President Trump said: ‘Okay, I will support the idea with Starlink.’ We greatly appreciate this,” Zelenskyy said.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb also assisted in advocating for the proposal, according to Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president said he had ultimately involved around 10 foreign leaders in efforts to secure Trump’s support.
The president also added Russia is developing an alternative to Starlink in cooperation with China and expects the system to be ready by December 2026.
At the same time, Ukraine is working with a European country on a separate communications project, which has already entered the testing stage. Zelenskyy stressed that while Ukraine intends to continue using Starlink, it is also developing European alternatives as part of broader efforts to prepare for emerging technological threats.
The discussions over Starlink come amid broader concerns over access to the satellite communications service for Ukraine. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski recently criticized Musk after Poland was removed from Starlink’s European roaming zone.
The decision raised concerns about its potential impact on satellite connectivity for Ukraine’s military, as Warsaw provides around $50 million annually to finance approximately half of the 42,000 Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine’s allies convene in Kyiv as Zelenskyy seeks air defence boost
articles.body:
Ukraine’s allies convene in Kyiv as Zelenskyy seeks air defence boost
‘Coalition of the Willing’ leaders gather on Independence Day as Kyiv presses for air defence supplies.
Ukraine will host a meeting with its key European allies to discuss air defence and press for greater pressure on Moscow as Russia continues to escalate missile attacks.
The “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in Kyiv on Monday will be jointly chaired by the leaders of the United Kingdom, France and Germany, with most leaders expected to join by video call and a small number of foreign dignitaries attending in person.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be in Kyiv for his first foreign trip since assuming office last month. European Council President Antonio Costa is also set to attend in person.
Kyiv is expected to seek additional interceptor missiles from allies after weeks of Russian missile and drone attacks that have driven record numbers of the capital city’s residents to metro stations and basements to seek shelter.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made frequent public appeals for more air defence supplies from allies.
The meeting takes place on Ukraine’s Independence Day and comes a day after the country marked National Flag Day, when a group of leaders from Nordic and Baltic countries met Zelenskyy in Kyiv and pledged to boost their support for Ukraine.
Norway said it would provide another 85 billion kroner ($9.1bn) in 2027, matching the support it gave Ukraine this year.
Escalating air attacks
Russia and Ukraine have escalated air attacks with drones and missiles in recent weeks, striking targets far beyond the front line.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian logistics sites, carrying out attacks on locations linked to e-commerce companies Wildberries and Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early on Monday at its warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.
Russian authorities said two children were killed and nine other people were wounded, including seven minors, when drone debris hit a private childcare centre in Krasnodar on Monday. Debris also fell on apartment buildings and set warehouses alight in the city, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
In the Stavropol region, which hosts many chemical production facilities, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said a drone attack on an industrial area had been repelled early on Monday.
In Ukraine, at least two women were killed and five people wounded when a Russian drone hit an electric train in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region on Sunday, regional officials said. An attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv city killed three people and injured eight.
Ukraine’s allies have pledged to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences in the face of Russia’s growing missile attacks.
Before the meeting, Zelenskyy said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” he said.
“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.

articles.title: WSJ: Russia holds mobilisation exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast
articles.body:
WSJ: Russia holds mobilisation exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast
Russian military officials conducted an exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast in July to test procedures for mobilising local residents.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing Western intelligence officials
Details: Western intelligence officials told the WSJ that Russian military officers had flown from St Petersburg to Kaliningrad Oblast last month, where they oversaw readiness planning and mobilisation procedures for local residents, including arrangements for their accommodation, food and weapons.
The exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast was just one of many such drills being held across Russia in preparation for a possible mobilisation.
The sources said the Kremlin has not yet decided whether to launch such measures and is unlikely to do so before the parliamentary elections at the end of September. However, Russian leader Vladimir Putin's determination to seize the entire Donbas could push him to take such a step.
The WSJ said that Moscow has failed in recent months to recruit enough new troops to replace battlefield losses, while the growing use of Ukrainian drones has "reduced the average Russian soldier's lifespan on the front to a matter of minutes, days or weeks". These manpower problems may leave Putin with no choice but to announce a new wave of mobilisation, US and European officials said.
Western intelligence also believes that, in the event of a possible escalation with the West, Russia could seize part of the Suwałki Gap, a strip of land linking Kaliningrad with Belarus through neighbouring Poland and Lithuania.
The WSJ reported that rumours of a possible new mobilisation have caused concern inside Russia in recent weeks and months, with men searching online for ways to leave the country in an emergency. Some Russians have already identified places where they could stay for several months to wait out a possible mobilisation.
A mobilisation could help reinforce Russia's line of contact and accelerate its advance towards Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in Donetsk Oblast. However, if it were launched this late in the year, before fighting slows in winter, it is unclear what practical effect the move would have.
Background: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 11 August that Russia is preparing to carry out additional mobilisation in the autumn after its sham parliamentary elections.

articles.title: 14 military targets and a second Ozon facility in two days: Ukraine intensifies strikes on Russia
articles.body:
14 military targets and a second Ozon facility in two days: Ukraine intensifies strikes on Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian forces struck 14 Russian military targets, including a Su-33, a MiG-29, an Orion UAV, radars, and an S-400 system. At the same time, the Armed Forces of Ukraine attacked an Ozon logistics hub in Orenburg — the company's second facility in two days.
Ukraine continues to systematically take out Russian aircraft, air defenses, and rear logistics. On August 23, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert "Madyar" Brovdi published a list of 14 successfully hit military targets, while in Orenburg the Ozon logistics hub came under attack for the second time in two days. Fire Point-produced weapons were used in both operations, UNN reports.
Details
The main part of Madyar's list consists of elements of Russia's air defense. It includes eight radar stations, two surface-to-air missile systems, and an S-400 "Triumf" position.
Thus, of the 14 targets named by Madyar, three were Russian aircraft, while another 11 were part of the enemy's detection and air defense system.
Ozon came under attack for the second time in two days
At the same time, on the morning of August 23, an FP-1 strike drone manufactured by Fire Point hit the logistics complex of the Russian marketplace Ozon in Orenburg. The use of an FP-1 was confirmed to UNN by Fire Point co-owner and chief designer Denys Shtilerman.
For Ozon, this is already the second attack in two days.
On August 22, Ukrainian FP-1 drones hit the company's logistics hub in Chapayevsk, Samara region. The Chapayevsk hub was one of Ozon's largest logistics centers in the Volga region. After all phases were launched, its area amounted to approximately 135,000 square meters, its capacity exceeded 40 million items, and the complex could process more than 215,000 orders per day.
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine explained the rationale behind the strikes on Russian logistics centers. The ministry emphasized that such facilities are used to store dual-use goods, and that systematically striking them complicates the enemy's logistics and hits the Russian economy.
After the strike on the hub in Chapayevsk, the Ministry of Defense stated that Ukrainian units had previously struck 15 of Wildberries' largest logistics hubs, and that now "it was Ozon's turn."
In fact, these are no longer isolated strikes on individual facilities. Ukraine is simultaneously taking out Russian air defense systems, aircraft, and infrastructure that ensures the movement of goods and supplies within the russian federation.

articles.title: Taiwan Navy to hold large-scale exercise next month
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Navy will conduct a large-scale exercise from Sept. 9 to 24 in waters off southeastern Taiwan.
According to a Fisheries Agency notice, the Navy will carry out live-fire drills against sea and air targets. They are scheduled for Sept. 9–10, 16–18, and 21–24.
No specific weapons were listed, but the notice said fighter jets, helicopters, and reconnaissance drones will be deployed.
The Navy has designated three warning zones. Zone 1 is located in waters east of Taimali in Taitung to Eluanbi in Pingtung. Zone 2 extends from the Taitung–Pingtung border eastward to waters off Green Island and Orchid Island. Zone 3 is situated in waters east of Chenggong and Taimali in Taitung.
In the past three years, the military has deployed a range of weapons during precision munitions live-fire drills, including Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles and Patriot and Sky Bow air defense missiles, per Liberty Times. Last year, the Kuai Chi attack unmanned surface vessel and Chien Hsiang-series attack drone were unveiled during drills.
The exercise announcement comes two weeks after China held navigation exercises, including communications and at-sea replenishment, with an Indonesian Navy frigate in waters east of the country. Taiwan's foreign ministry condemned the move, saying that China disregarded “international norms and responsibilities” and escalated regional tensions.
There has been an increase in Chinese gray zone and military activities near Taiwan’s eastern waters this year. In late July, Chinese coast guard vessels, the Xiushan and Chongming, were found 280 kilometers and 80 km east of Lanyu, respectively. The Chinese coast guard claimed they were conducting a routine law enforcement mission.
National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said in July that China has deployed a record of more than 110 military and coast guard ships along the First Island Chain.

articles.title: Independence Day gift from inside Russian army: Partisans say soldier whose comrades were killed over extortion money destroyed truck resupplying Kostiantynivka front
articles.body:
Ukrainian partisans have dedicated their new “catch” to Ukraine’s Independence Day. According to ATESH, they destroyed a military KamAZ truck that was used in assaults on Donetsk Oblast and was stationed with Russian occupation forces in Rostov Oblast.
ATESH is a Ukrainian-Crimean Tatar partisan movement founded in September 2022 in response to Russia's full-scale invasion. The group operates in occupied Ukrainian territories and in Russia itself, with members including Crimean Tatars, Ukrainians, and Russians who were mobilized into the Russian army but now work for Ukraine.
The operation was carried out without the partisans even having to do it themselves. The vehicle was used in the offensive toward Kostiantynivka, one of the hottest sectors of the current fighting, alongside the Russian advances toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
The sabotage was carried out by a soldier from the Russian Armed Forces’ “Center” Group of Forces, which is assaulting Kostiantynivka. The vehicle was actively used to supply the advancing forces, and its loss disrupts Russian logistics.
Putin has a primary target, Zelenskyy says
Earlier, President Zelenskyy said that the offensive toward Kostiantynivka would remain one of the Russian military’s main priorities through the end of the year, according to Suspilne.
“Putin’s unchanged primary objective on the front is Kostiantynivka–Sloviansk. The latest deadline he has given his generals is to complete the occupation of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by the end of the year,” he said.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russia has lost 267,000 personnel along the entire front line, including approximately 155,000 killed, according to the figures cited in the report. Russian forces are suffering their heaviest losses specifically in the sector stretching from Sloviansk to Kostiantynivka.
How was the operation carried out?
The agent joined the movement out of revenge: his commanders killed his fellow soldiers after he refused to pay extortionate demands. The partisans said that such abuses in the Russian army are commonplace, and that the only way to survive and punish those responsible is to resist from within.
Earlier, the partisans reported that Russia’s 64th Motor Rifle Brigade, which has been implicated in crimes in Bucha, was concealing its actual losses. The command allegedly registers many of the dead as “missing in action” in order to reduce the official death toll and avoid payments to their families.
Meanwhile, security and counterintelligence services are reportedly putting pressure on the women, threatening them with criminal charges for “discrediting” the army and the complete loss of any payments if they continue searching for their missing relatives.

articles.title: Britain clears Storm Shadow missile assembly in Ukraine
articles.body:
Britain has approved the release of classified UK missile technology to help France and Ukraine establish local assembly of the Storm Shadow long-range cruise missile.
Britain has authorised MBDA to release classified technical information on UK components used in the Storm Shadow/SCALP missile family, removing a British-controlled barrier to plans for long-range cruise missiles to be assembled inside Ukraine, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The decision was announced ahead of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s visit to Kyiv on 24 August, his first overseas trip since entering Downing Street. Under the approval, MBDA will be permitted to share protected information covering British elements of the Franco-British missile design so that France and Ukraine can move forward with plans to establish local assembly lines.
Storm Shadow is the British designation for the long-range air-launched cruise missile, while France operates the closely related weapon as SCALP. Both are designed to strike important fixed targets at considerable distance, allowing the launch aircraft to release the weapon well away from the target area before the missile flies towards it at low altitude. The UK became the first country to provide Ukraine with Western long-range strike missiles when it supplied Storm Shadow in 2023.
The latest move goes further than simply transferring completed weapons from existing stocks. By allowing protected British information to be released, London is supporting French and Ukrainian efforts to establish part of the missile’s assembly process inside Ukraine itself.
According to a Downing Street news update, the decision will allow France and Ukraine to proceed with Ukrainian assembly of the missile. It follows efforts by Kyiv and Paris to expand local production of long-range weapons and is intended to give Ukraine greater ability to sustain its strike capability without relying entirely on deliveries of complete missiles from abroad.
The Government said the decision also complements Project Brakestop, a separate UK-led effort to rapidly develop lower-cost advanced long-range strike weapons for Ukraine. That gives British support two distinct missile-related strands: helping Ukraine gain access to the technology needed for local assembly of an established Franco-British cruise missile, while also pursuing newer weapons intended to be produced more cheaply and at greater scale.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.”
He added: “I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.”
Burnham is expected to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv and co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing alongside other leaders attending Ukrainian Independence Day events. Britain and France jointly lead the coalition, while the UK says its support for Ukraine has so far included £25 billion in funding, including £16 billion in military assistance.
Burnham said: “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

articles.title: Syria tells Israel it won't limit military buildup in security deal talks
articles.body:
Syria told Israel that it would not accept restrictions on its right to develop its military capabilities or form alliances with other countries as part of a future security arrangement, Syria's state-run SANA news agency reported Sunday night, citing a diplomatic source.
According to the source, talks between the two countries focused on developing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli strikes in Syria and reviving negotiations toward a security agreement that could eventually serve as the basis for a broader accord.
SANA reported that Damascus stressed that it would reject any mechanisms limiting Syrian sovereignty. Its immediate priority, according to the report, is the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines held before December 8, 2024, and the full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement. The diplomatic source said any future security arrangement must also respect Syria's territorial integrity.
The report came after Mossad Chief Roman Gofman met with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Sunday in an effort to defuse tensions between the two countries following Israel's strike on Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Reuters reported last week that Gofman and al-Shaibani had also spoken by phone several days before the strike and discussed Turkey's military presence in Syria. Axios first reported Sunday's meeting, citing two sources familiar with the matter.
In an interview with Reuters on Saturday, al-Shaibani said negotiations over a security agreement with Israel had been frozen since the start of the Iran war and that contact between the two countries was cut following the airbase strike. He nevertheless said he expected negotiations to resume soon and hoped an agreement would ultimately lead to Israel's withdrawal from Syrian territory.
Al-Shaibani said the United States was continuously pressing Israel to return to negotiations and urged Israel to seize what he called a "historic opportunity" while the door to diplomacy remains open. He said Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks and that confidence-building measures are needed.
"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn't bring results, then we don't need it," al-Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
Asked about the prospects for an agreement, al-Shaibani said it was "very hard to bet on Israel," but that Syria had "very great hope" of establishing stable relations with its neighbors. "Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability, he said.
Israel said following the strike that Damascus was preparing to allow Turkish forces to deploy at the airbase. Syria and Turkey denied the claim, and al-Shaibani said Israel struck the base even after Syria conveyed that it would not be used as a Turkish base.
Al-Shaibani said Syria receives training and military assistance from Turkey, as well as support from Jordan, Saudi Arabia and other countries. He said Damascus was grateful for Turkey's help in rebuilding the Syrian military and "will not give up that support."
Washington has sought for more than a year to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The talks have yet to produce an agreement amid Israeli strikes on Syrian government assets and the deployment of Israeli troops inside Syrian territory, which Israel says are necessary for its security.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office did not respond to al-Shaibani's remarks.

articles.title: The Supreme Court Let Trump’s Ballroom Proceed—for Now. Here’s What That Means
articles.body:
The U.S. Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump to continue construction on a new White House ballroom with a temporary stay issued Friday—just before the aboveground portion of the project was about to be halted.
Chief Justice John Roberts, in a one-sentence order, stayed a federal district court judge’s injunction that barred further development. The move gives the full Supreme Court more time to consider the Trump Administration’s request to keep the injunction on hold while it seeks further review. However, there is no established timeline for when Roberts or the Court might take further action.
The ruling comes after months of debate over a legal challenge brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argues that a President cannot unilaterally make a major, permanent change to federally owned property when Congress has not authorized it, pointing toward the Property Clause of the Constitution.
“We reiterated that the Administration has no unilateral legal authority—constitutional, statutory, or otherwise—to build a Ballroom on the site of the now-demolished East Wing, unless and until Congress expressly approves,” the National Trust for Historic Preservation said in a statement last week. “Each court that has reviewed this case has agreed with the National Trust. We hope the Supreme Court will uphold the rule of law by stopping this illegal project.”
Read More: What to Know About Trump’s Aide Natalie Harp
Trump reacted to the administrative stay on Truth Social on Friday, praising both the Supreme Court and Roberts, who was appointed by former President George W. Bush in 2005.
“We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court,” Trump said. “The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!”
Here’s what to know about the latest updates on the $400 million project.
How did the ballroom case reach the Supreme Court?
Two lower-court decisions brought the dispute before the Supreme Court.
First, Senior Judge Richard Leon of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that the National Trust was likely to succeed on its claim that the project required congressional approval, and he ruled in March that construction on the aboveground ballroom could not take place while litigation continued. He modified that preliminary injunction on April 16 to clarify that security-related work could continue if it is "strictly necessary to ensure the safety and security of the White House.”
The second decision came when the Trump Administration appealed, and a D.C. Circuit panel upheld the modified injunction. In its August ruling, it said that each President is a “temporary tenant, not the owner,” of the White House.
According to Kimberly Wehle, professor of law at the University of Baltimore School of Law, the injunction is meant to ensure that the project does not advance while the courts review its legality, the limits of presidential authority, and whether it might cause irreparable harm.
“The court is saying, ‘We just need to stop the bleeding right now, because if this continues, it'll just cause more harm,’” she tells TIME.
The Trump Administration then asked the Supreme Court to intervene through an emergency application, which is meant for urgent review of time-sensitive matters that fall outside of the typically months- or years-long case review timeline for the country’s highest court.
The case was put in front of Roberts, who oversees emergency appeals filed in the D.C. Circuit.
That led to the administrative stay—a short-term order that freezes a lower court decision or deadline in order to buy time for a bench to review an emergency request. An administrative stay does not reflect a case’s merits or legality; it acts as an interim measure for a future ruling from Roberts or the Court.
In this case, it paused the preliminary injunction originally handed down by Leon. Therefore, the stop-work order was put aside for the time being, allowing construction to continue.
"We are aware of the administrative stay," the National Trust tells TIME, in response to the latest developments. "To be clear, this is not a final decision on the merits of the government’s stay application, and we await further action.”
No court has issued a final ruling on the project’s legality. But next steps will likely include determining whether the renovation is two distinct projects—aboveground and below—or a singular build.
Is Trump building a ballroom or a military complex?
Trump’s 90,000-square-foot construction project comprises a luxury ballroom—which is meant to host 650 seated guests—with an underground military complex beneath it, featuring “protective missile resistant steel columns, beams, drone proof roofing materials, and bullet, ballistic, and blast proof glass,” according to one court document.
Lower courts treated the two components separately, finding that the National Trust was likely to establish that the aboveground ballroom required congressional approval while exempting underground security construction from the injunction.
In making his injunction determination, Leon said: “Defendants themselves distinguished between below-ground and above-ground construction, stating that ‘the below-surface work is driven by national security concerns independent of the above-grade construction.’”
Leon and the D.C. Circuit said the Administration had shifted from treating the components as independent to describing them as inseparable. The Administration disputes that characterization, saying the design became less flexible as construction progressed. It now argues that the entire project is integrated and that halting the aboveground work would compromise its structural integrity and security functions.
“Every day the President does not have access to the vital security features of the military complex presents unacceptable risk, no matter how long the Project takes to complete,” Solicitor General John Sauer argued in court filings last week. “Built with integrated engineering, the Project will provide in a very large way, a ‘safe room’ for the Presidency and the continuity of government.”
Presidents in the past have relied on the White House’s Presidential Emergency Operations Center (PEOC), which dates to World War II, as a safe room or bunker. The Administration has argued that the former East Wing’s security infrastructure had become vulnerable to modern threats, including drones and missiles, making the new construction urgent.
In court documents, it claimed the former building “cannot protect guests against inclement weather, let alone high-powered weapons.”
The White House in August shared AI-generated images of drones, military personnel, and vehicles on the roof of the ballroom. Trump has claimed that a “drone port” will feature a launching deck and defense station.
He told reporters in March on Air Force One that the ballroom would become a “shed for what’s being built under” and that it would have its own security features, such as bulletproof glass.
Whether or not the two components are accepted as a single entity, from a legal standpoint, could determine the outcome of the outstanding emergency relief.
Could construction outrun judicial review?
In Trump’s post on social media Friday, he said that construction of the ballroom “is under budget and ahead of schedule.”
The Administration claimed in its Aug. 13 application that 65% of construction was done. When the project was announced in 2025, the White House said that construction would be done “long before the end of President Trump’s term.” The Administration is now saying that the framework will be substantially complete by November, with the official completion date set for August 2028, according to appendixes to the emergency application that was submitted by the Trump Administration.
This raises the question of whether a majority of the structure could be completed before the litigation is resolved.
Lawyers for the National Trust accused the Trump Administration in a court filing earlier this month of “trying to outrun judicial review,” pointing to the Administration’s own assertion that the structure will soon be “virtually impossible to deconstruct.”
Wehle says that Roberts’s stay is “giving Trump exactly what he wants” by allowing him to get ever closer to the project’s completion while the courts assess whether he is breaking the law.
“This is the Supreme Court greenlighting unconstitutional, lawless behavior by the President,” Wehle says. She questions whether the President is being accommodated because it seemed like the project had gone too far and might be harder to undo at this point than to simply finish—especially when weighing the potential harm to the public in terms of cost, damage, and timeline.
But if that’s true, she asks, “What kind of precedent does that set?”
“That is a precedent that says the law is optional,” she explains. That could embolden a strategy of acting first and asking permission second, if at all.
If the project were ultimately found unlawful after construction was substantially or entirely complete, the case could present unusual questions about what remedy remained available—including whether a court could order the structure altered, reverted, or removed.

articles.body:

Ukraine’s Armed Robot Rolls Into Russian Position and Opens Fire, Killing 20, Video
Ukrainian troops used an armed unmanned ground vehicle to attack a Russian-held position without sending soldiers into direct-fire range, killing 20 Russian troops, according to Ukrainian defense technology company DevDroid.
Soldiers from Ukraine’s 44th Separate Mechanized Brigade carried out the operation using the company’s Droid TW-12.7 strike UGV, DevDroid said in an August 21 press release.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian troops had taken shelter inside a building at one of their positions, according to the company. Ukrainian operators remotely drove the ground robot toward the structure before opening fire with its remotely controlled combat module armed with a 12.7 mm (.50-caliber) M2 Browning heavy machine gun.
DevDroid said the position was neutralized and 20 Russian troops were killed during the engagement. The casualty figure could not be independently verified.
The entire attack was conducted remotely.
Instead of Ukrainian infantry having to approach the Russian position under fire, the Droid TW-12.7 performed the most dangerous part of the mission itself—closing the distance to the target and engaging the troops inside with direct machine-gun fire.
Developed by Ukrainian engineers at DevDroid, the Droid TW-12.7 was designed as a combined reconnaissance and strike platform capable of operating close to frontline positions.
Its remotely operated weapons system is paired with onboard cameras, a ballistic computer and AI-assisted functions designed to help operators detect, track and engage targets while remaining away from the immediate combat zone.
The vehicle’s M2 Browning gives it substantial firepower for a relatively compact unmanned platform. The heavy machine gun can be used against infantry, firing positions, unarmored vehicles and some lightly armored targets.
The Droid can also provide remote battlefield surveillance, transmitting video and other data to its operators in real time and allowing Ukrainian troops to observe hostile positions without physically moving into exposed areas.
That combination allows the platform to support both offensive and defensive missions—from reconnaissance and fire support to direct attacks on fortified positions in areas where sending troops forward could carry a high risk of casualties.
The Droid TW-12.7 is built for mobility across rough terrain and off-road conditions and has already been tested in combat environments.
Previously, an armed Ukrainian ground robot was carried across the water by an uncrewed maritime platform, landed on the Russian-held Kinburn Spit, and sent into combat—an operation the military described as the first known mission of its kind anywhere in the world.

articles.title: Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.
The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time to a demand made by the sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.
“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.
Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.
That shifted when Fedorov, a popular minister who had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.
It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.
Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”
Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.
Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.
“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors in 2027--28.
The US could help by supplying “some small percentage” of its stockpiles – about 5% to 10%, he added. Ukraine was willing to pay and it would mean the country “could get through the winter”, he said, calling on the US to make what would be “a very significant difference both in protecting lives and diplomatically”.
Following a conversation with Zelenskyy on Saturday, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had agreed to strengthen French support for Ukraine, including through the delivery of interceptor missiles, without giving further details.
Ukraine’s allies in the so-called coalition of the willing – an initiative led by France and Britain – will meet on Monday to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.
Russia is seeking to build up forces for a renewed effort to capture the rest of the eastern Donetsk province it does not control by the end of the year, though Zelenskyy said he was confident Moscow would fail to capture the area, comprising principally the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The president said he believed Russia would try to conscript a further 300,000 soldiers after the Russian parliamentary elections in September. It would be a “peripheral mobilisation” conducted away from Moscow, St Petersburg and other main cities in an effort to regain momentum in the almost deadlocked frontline, he said.

articles.title: US-Israeli strikes hit medical and nuclear facilities, Iran nuclear chief says
articles.body:
US-Israeli strikes hit medical and nuclear facilities, Iran nuclear chief says
TEHRAN- The head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization (AEOI), Mohammad Eslami, said US and Israeli military strikes over the past year targeted facilities linked not only to Iran’s nuclear program but also to the production of medical and diagnostic materials used by patients across the country.
Speaking at a ceremony marking Physicians’ Day in Iran’s nuclear industry on Sunday, Eslami said the nuclear fuel production plant in Isfahan was the first facility targeted during the attacks. The plant produces fuel for the Tehran Research Reactor, which is primarily used for research and the production of radiopharmaceuticals.
Eslami said a radiopharmaceutical production facility was also hit in the air raids, while an oxygen-18 production line at the Khondab complex was bombed. Oxygen-18 is used in positron emission tomography (PET) scans, a key diagnostic tool in modern medicine.
He said AEOI-produced medical and diagnostic products are used by more than 1.5 million people in Iran each year and are also exported to several countries. Eslami argued that the targeting of facilities involved in scientific and medical production demonstrated the consequences of the attacks beyond the nuclear sector.
“Scientific activities whose products are used by the public” were among the targets, Eslami said, describing the strikes as a clear reflection of the attackers’ approach toward Iran’s scientific capabilities.
Eslami also highlighted Iran’s development of cold plasma technology, describing it as a promising new avenue for medical applications. According to the AEOI chief, more than 20 wound-treatment clinics across Iran are currently using the technology in treatments aimed at cancer patients and pain relief.
The remarks underscore the overlap between Iran’s civilian nuclear program and its broader medical and scientific infrastructure, particularly in areas such as radiopharmaceuticals and nuclear medicine. Tehran has repeatedly emphasized the medical and research applications of its nuclear capabilities, while the United States and Israel have targeted parts of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure during their military confrontations with the country.
Eslami said Iran’s nuclear industry has continued to develop medical technologies despite the attacks, with researchers pursuing advanced applications in healthcare and expanding the international reach of domestically produced nuclear-related medical products.

articles.title: 3 children killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Ozon warehouse in southern Russia
articles.body:

At least three children were killed and seven others injured after debris from a Ukrainian drone, targeting the warehouse of an e-commerce company Ozon, fell on a private children’s center in Russia's southern city of Krasnodar, Russian authorities said on Monday.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Russian social media platform Max that initially the drone was shot down by air defenses during a large-scale attack overnight.
Russian Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova confirmed the death toll.
"A terrible tragedy in Krasnodar Krai. Last night, as a result of a massive Ukrainian attack, according to preliminary information, three teenagers — aged 13, 15, and 16 — were killed," she said in a statement on Max.
The overnight attacks also targeted several Ozon logistics facilities across southern Russia.
Ozon said its facilities in Adygeysk in the Adygea region, Makhachkala in Dagestan and Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region came under drone attack.
Employees were evacuated from the Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk facilities because of the threat of further attacks.
Ozon also confirmed that its logistics center in Krasnodar was attacked. The company had earlier said a fire broke out at the facility.
A separate Ozon logistics center in the Takhtamukaysky district of Adygea also caught fire following a drone attack, according to Russian authorities.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said it carried out overnight strikes on Ukrainian port infrastructure and vessels used to deliver supplies to the Ukrainian military.
The Russian Defense Ministry said strikes hit the port of Pivdennyi in Ukraine’s Odesa region, including a tanker carrying fuel intended for Ukrainian forces, five fuel storage tanks, 10 storage facilities containing military-related equipment and port infrastructure used to unload and store military cargo.
Russia also said it had struck the Adzhalyk-330 substation, about 28 kilometers (17.3 miles) northwest of Odesa, which it said sends supplies to Pivdennyi Port.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks interceptor missiles from Japan: Report
articles.body:
Riyaz ul Khaliq
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Ukraine is seeking interceptor missiles from Japan, the war-torn nation’s prime minister has said.
“I would like to kindly ask one and only thing ... anti-ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi told Kyodo News in an interview released on Monday.
Koretskyi “expressed hope that Japan will provide Kyiv with air defense systems.”
The Russia-Ukraine war has been ongoing since February 2022.
“It's the most important thing we need to protect our people, infrastructure ... through this (winter) heating season," Koretskyi said about the interceptor missiles.
“I very much hope (for) and count on your country," he told the Japanese news agency.
Ukraine is supplied with Patriot interceptor missiles by a coalition of Western nations, but its stockpile has been depleting.
Japan, a defense ally of the US, is one of the manufacturers of the Patriot surface-to-air missile interceptors under a US license, the report added.
However, Japanese arms exports, under the country’s three principles on the transfer of defense equipment and technology, “to countries in which conflicts are taking place is, (are) in principle, prohibited.”
In April, Tokyo revised limits on defense equipment exports.
The revised terms “on the transfer of defense equipment and technology require countries to sign agreements with Japan on protecting related classified information to be eligible for the transfer of lethal weapons,” it said.
“Even if an agreement for the transfer of defense equipment and technology is signed, the provision of interceptor missiles would need to be green-lighted by (Prime Minister Sanae) Takaichi,” according to Kyodo News.
Koretskyi said: "I do believe in our bright future and cooperation and partnership regarding the reconstruction and development of our country. Even now, we do not want to wait before the war (is) over.”

articles.title: Nausėda Assures Ukraine of Continued Military and EU Integration Support

“For Lithuania, it is very important to remain consistent. We signed an agreement on my country’s annual support, which will be no less than 0.25% of our GDP each year. “So together with you, with your help and support, we are better prepared to meet all these challenges, confront them, and deal with them much more successfully,” the Lithuanian president stressed.
He also placed particular emphasis on his “special attitude” toward Ukraine’s integration into the European Union.

Details: In his post marking the holiday, Mykhailo Drapatyi, Commander-in-Chief of Ukraine's Armed Forces, observed that the flag is not only in Ukrainians' hearts, but also on their uniforms.
"Thanks to Ukraine's Armed Forces, the blue-and-yellow flag has become a symbol of struggle, resilience and will to the whole world. We will do everything possible to make this flag the flag of victory," the commander-in-chief said.
The National Guard's 1st Azov Corps marked the holiday by posting a video about the meaning of the national flag for Ukrainians during wartime.
"Independence has its visible expressions, and among them the flag holds a special place," the unit said. "This is a flag with centuries of struggle and the blood of heroes behind it. Colours that people eagerly look out for as they return home from foreign lands and captivity. A symbol that unites all Ukrainians without the need for words. It has been saved from fire, preserved in exile, smuggled out of occupation. The flag that flies over our shared home. The colours that unite us."
The 93rd Kholodnyi Yar Separate Mechanised Brigade noted that the flag "passes through fire" alongside Ukrainian troops, and so carries the marks of war and evidence of the defenders' resilience.
"For every citizen it is an honour to raise and live under their own flag, but for Ukrainians this opportunity comes through an arduous struggle," the unit said. "This flag represents our land, our freedom, and our memory of those who paid the ultimate price. That is exactly why the enemy is prepared to throw everything into destroying the Ukrainian flag – to tear it down, burn it, throw it off buildings. Because they know that it isn't just a piece of fabric. As long as the Ukrainian flag flies over the land, that land remains Ukrainian. And wherever it is raised again, Ukraine returns."
Among the symbolic flags Ukrainians recall on this day is a tattered one found in a vehicle that survived a shelling near Ilovaisk on 29 August 2014.
Vatra, a military and volunteer community, recounted the flag's history: "During the withdrawal from the Ilovaisk encirclement on 29 August 2014, the flag was in a ZiL-131 truck carrying an anti-aircraft mount. The vehicle came under fire, two soldiers were killed, and the others got into a surviving vehicle from the 93rd Brigade. They were later captured by Russian forces. The tattered flag was found in the burnt-out vehicle by a search team from the Evacuation 200 (Black Tulip) mission while searching for fallen Ukrainian soldiers in September 2014."
Members of special police units posted photos taken with the state flag at their combat positions.
"For the fighters of our special police unit, the state flag is a symbol of freedom, honour and the unbreakable spirit of the Ukrainian people. Under the flag we carry out combat missions, hold our positions, support our brothers-in-arms, and continue the fight for every metre of Ukrainian land," the soldiers wrote. "And wherever we are – at our positions, in the skies or on the ground – we know what we're standing for. May the blue-and-yellow flag always fly over a free and independent Ukraine."
The National Council of Ukraine for Television and Radio Broadcasting shared moments from the archives relating to the blue-and-yellow flag's establishment as a national symbol.
The Defence Ministry's online media outlet, Army TV, recalled that during Soviet times, people were persecuted and imprisoned for the sake of the Ukrainian flag, recalling one such incident from 1966 when student Heorhii Moskalenko and worker Viktor Kuksa raised a blue-and-yellow flag made out of two scarves over the Kyiv Institute of National Economy.
"Kuksa cut down the red flag and put up the Ukrainian one. It flew over Kyiv for several hours," Army TV said. "The KGB searched for them for nine months. Moskalenko was sentenced to three years in a strict-regime labour camp, Kuksa to two. They continued to be monitored after their release. Both were only rehabilitated in 2007."
The Security Service of Ukraine noted: "For many generations, [the flag] has been the symbol of a stolen dream and boundless strength of spirit. For the sake of the flag people were persecuted, their homes searched, criminal cases opened against them, and they were intimidated and killed. Yet despite this, Ukrainians continued to preserve and raise their flag."
